title: 13 Contestants of the 2026 Hiri Hanenamo are preparing for the official crowning
content:
As the Boge-Bada reached the shores of Era Kone(Ela Beach), the voices of the Hiri Hanenamos shouting the famous ‘Hedi-horo Boge-bada’ echoed along the shoreline of Era Kone.
The 13 contestants are participating in the Hiri Hanenamo Quest, which is the prestigious cultural pageant held during the annual Hiri Moale Festival in Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea.
The 13 contestants, after their official registration had participated in different judging categories, lead-up events and community engagement within their communities, have now reached the peak of the quest, which is the crowning, that will be staged tomorrow, September 13, 2026, at the Sir Herbert Murray Stadium after the last sway (Koea).
Unlike a conventional pageant, the Hiri Hanenamo focuses rigorously on cultural literacy, community leadership, and the preservation of the historic Hiri trade legacy.
These exemplary young women have been formally nominated by their respective local leaders to serve as cultural ambassadors, representing the identity, oral history, and traditional values of their respective Motu and Koitabu villages.
The annual event is organised by the Motu Koita Assembly, in collaboration with the National Capital District Commission and the Hiri Moale Festival Committee.
The 13 contestants for the 2026 quest are:
• Hanenamo 1: Miss Asi Hota — Gaire
• Hanenamo 2: Miss Edna Moi Oala — Boera
• Hanenamo 3: Miss Keruma Asi — Porebada
• Hanenamo 4: Miss Mary Ruth Kua — Elevala Lahara
• Hanenamo 5: Miss Margaret Mulaseula — Kouderika
• Hanenamo 6: Miss Matlinge Nanai — Pari Taurama
• Hanenamo 7: Miss Latasha Gari — Elevala Laurabada
• Hanenamo 8: Miss Hoeke Allen — Korobosea
• Hanenamo 9: Miss Tyla Aua — Boera
• Hanenamo 10: Miss Judith Julie Gadiki — Kira Kira
• Hanenamo 11: Miss Boio Buri — Pari Taurama
• Hanenamo 12: Miss Cheryl Solien — Araira
• Hanenamo 13: Miss Faith Hale Mataio — Pari Taoata
The 2026 Hiri Moale Festival program is scheduled to run from Tuesday September 8th to Sunday, 13th September 2026.

title: 'What's good for Māori is good for Tangata Moana': Pacific solidarity strong at Koroneihana
content:
'What's good for Māori is good for Tangata Moana': Pacific solidarity strong at Koroneihana
More than friends, but whānau - that's the recurring message from Māori to Pacific people on the third day of Koroneihana.
This comes as delegates and community members from across the Pacific gathered at Tūrangawaewae marae today, honouring reigning Māori Queen Te Arikinui Kuini Nga wai hono i te po.
Year after year, Koroneihana serves as a meeting point for Māori and the wider Pacific, bringing together leaders and community representatives from all over the Moana.
Kiingitanga spokesperson Rahui Papa said those longstanding and special relationships continue to underpin the connection between Māori and their Pacific neighbours.
Many Pacific peoples call Aotearoa home, and so it's a priority for those relationships to be nurtured, Papa said.
"There's a lot of our whānau from the Pacific. They live here in Aotearoa, and there's a whole lot of relationships that have been built up over many years," he said.
"So, I think it's going to be more about grounding the relationship first, and then those pieces of work can flow from that foundation."
Speaking on the paepae, Papa emphasised that the attendance of Fiji's paramount chief of Lau Province, Ratu Tevita Kapaiwai Lutunauga Uluilakeba Mara, and Tonga's Princess Lātūfuipeka reinforced that bond.
"It's more than just 'cousins' of the Pacific. It's more, family of the Pacific, tēnā koutou," Papa said.
That sentiment was echoed by Green Party candidate Michel Mulipola, who said Pacific peoples play a critical role in standing alongside Māori.
"It's important that we stand with our cousins of the Moana, you know, in solidarity to support them in their rights," Mulipola said.
"What's good for Māori is also good for tangata moana, and so for me it's very important to be part of these procedures because we need to have that connection, together in solidarity."
The Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick also spoke about the merits of focussing on commonalities.
"We're all aware of the things that could divide us," she said.
"But if we just spend a moment to actually fixate on the things that could bring us together, on the things that are so amazing and beautiful about this country, and we work on building those things up, we're unstoppable."
Jordan Nonoa, who spoke on behalf of the Hamilton Pacific Community Association, emphasised the unity.
"Keeping those relationships strong is all part of it. There's so many moving parts behind it, and for all of us showing up and turning out, we just keep it going, that cycle moving forward."
The same message was reflected among many Pasifika rangatahi and community leaders.
Sister Funaki, a youth representative from Tonga, said the sense of connection across the Pacific was impossible to miss.
"One of the things I love about today, similar to all the cultures in the South Pacific, we're all from one moana, is the love, the warmth and the joy that everyone brings here today in support of the Māori Queen," Funaki said.
Performer Rayna Folau, who was representing Pacific Advance Secondary School, said attending Koroneihana was also about carrying those relationships into the future.
"I believe it's really important to come to events like this, because we are the youth and the future generation for events like this, so I just feel really grateful," Folau said.
Her kaiako, Petuleka Malelei, said the presence of young Pasifika was a sign those connections would endure.
"It's important they are here," Malelei said.
"We as a Pacific voice want to make sure our presence is always felt, in support of the Kiingitanga and the movement, and all the projects that happen under te ao Māori, that the moana is always in presence and support."
Community member Vai Filimoehala was among those representing Tonga.
Alongside colleagues, she presented a tapa as koha, a piece handcrafted by members of her community back home.
Representing the Tongan royal family, Filimoehala said the gift carried deep significance.
The tapa featured a crown motif and Tonga's royal shield and was made collectively by women in her village.
"It was made back in my village by my grandmothers, aunties and them. It takes a village to make it," she said.
Attention now turns to tomorrow's annual address from the Māori Queen, with thousands expected to gather for one of the event's most anticipated moments.

title: The ‘National Park’ That Stretches From Coast to Coast
content:
On Doug Tallamy’s 10-acre property in rural Pennsylvania, the evidence arrives on wings. Wood thrushes now nest in shrubs that were once cut for hay. Luna moths — emerald-green giants that had become increasingly rare — have reached record numbers. Tallamy recounts enthusiastically that he has documented more than 1,380 species of moths on the land, along with 62 breeding bird species. “We hear the birds in the morning. I see the gray tree frog sitting on my window sill,” he raves. “That is a real reward for me.”
When he and his wife Cindy bought the 300-year-old farm in 2000, its surroundings looked green. But when Tallamy walked the property he noticed it was overrun by invasive plants — like the Japanese stiltgrass and the aptly named mile-a-minute-weed, a smothering vine — that supported few pollinators. “There were no caterpillars!” he recalls. That recognition turned him from a researcher with a passion for insects into a passionate advocate for native plants. The transformation of his land didn’t require expensive engineering or high-tech equipment. Tallamy simply weeded out invasives and put native plants back. “I think in the last 26 years we spent about $100,” he says. “Because I simply go get seeds and put them in the ground.”
For more than two decades, the bestselling author and entomologist at the University of Delaware has argued that the biodiversity crisis won’t be solved only in national parks or on other protected lands. It will be solved — or lost — in millions of ordinary backyards and schoolyards, on corporate campuses and apartment balconies. “Nearly 80 percent of land east of the Mississippi is privately owned, and 135 million acres are now in residential landscapes,” he says. “That puts the private property owner in charge of conservation. If 10 to 20 percent of landowners planted native plants, this would add up to a habitat larger than 10 Yellowstones.”
National parks are much needed and beloved, but Tallamy points out that many species migrate beyond their borders and won’t survive if they don’t find sustenance and habitat along the way. “In between protected areas is no man’s land for most creatures and plants,” he says. “All of the parks and preserves, including Yellowstone, are too small and too isolated.” Connecting those islands with habitat on private land, he argues, “is going to be the solution.”
This premise led to his creation of Homegrown National Park, a nonprofit that encourages people to replace conventional lawns with native habitat and register their efforts on a nationwide biodiversity map. The initiative has now grown to over 52,000 registered participants who tend to more than 187,000 acres, figures Tallamy says are rapidly rising. “The real argument is that natural systems are generating your life support,” he urges. “They make your oxygen, they manage your watershed, they minimize extreme weather conditions, sequester carbon to help [mitigate] climate change. They’re doing all kinds of things to keep you alive on this planet.”
While the current administration guts the Endangered Species Act, reduces national monuments, defunds national parks and opens millions of acres of public lands to drilling and grazing, Tallamy is urging every American to give nature a boost where they can. “Everything we plant, don’t plant, or apply to our yard impacts the greater ecosystem in which our yard exists, and thus everything that depends on that ecosystem,” he writes in his most recent book, How Can I Help? Saving Nature with Your Yard. He argues that we don’t have the luxury to ignore that simple truth. “Everybody requires healthy ecosystems whether they know it or not,” he says. “That means it’s everybody’s responsibility to contribute to taking care of these systems.”
Tallamy emphasizes the urgency: “When you read that we’ve lost three billion breeding birds and have 22 percent fewer butterflies just since the year 2000, global insect decline, two-thirds of wildlife gone — that’s upsetting to a lot of people,” he says. “Even if they don’t know anything about biology, they don’t want to hear that everything on the planet is dying.”

Rather than stopping there, Tallamy pivots toward agency. “Our simple message is: There are things you can do. You can see the results. It empowers you to be part of the solution instead of part of the problem.” He argues that the reward of taking action is immediate: “If you plant an oak tree in your yard, you can see the difference tomorrow.”
Homegrown National Park’s website and Tallamy’s books give detailed practical advice on what anybody can do, from planting keystone species to shrinking one’s lawn and leaving the leaves as shelter for pollinators. But even people without a yard can find plenty of useful information. “If everybody did container gardening on their balcony, it [would become] a resource for native bee species in cities,” he says. “Migrating monarchs will use these plants.” And if someone really does not want to handle plants, Tallamy has hands-on advice for them, too: “Then change the light bulb outside from a white bulb to an amber bulb to stop killing moths all night long. You don’t need a PhD to do that, but it would make a huge difference.”
Whether this grassroots movement can scale fast enough to make a measurable ecological difference remains an open question. But as governments struggle to halt biodiversity loss, Tallamy is betting on changing culture.
Referring to the U.N.’s initiative of conserving 30 percent of land and water by 2030, commonly referred to as 30 x 30, he says, “You’ve got to count what’s happening on private property. And nobody’s doing that. Nobody’s recording it. That’s what that biodiversity map is all about.”
In his books, which have sold over half a million copies, Tallamy propagates a stubbornly upbeat view. “The cultural change from an adversarial relationship with nature to a collaborative one is starting to happen,” he writes in his latest book, “and it gives me hope about the future of biodiversity and thus our own future.”
Tallamy’s initiative is especially trying to reach people not usually interested in ecosystem health. “That is of course most people,” he acknowledges. “We try to create a social network to motivate people who don’t have a clue, who don’t know they are responsible for good earth stewardship right where they live.” He tours the country relentlessly giving speeches “and there is usually someone who has been dragged in by their neighbor.”
In parts of the Deep South, Tallamy says, traditional landscaping culture remains resistant to rewilding. Many homeowners associate tidy lawns with safety and social acceptance.
Tallamy is refreshingly candid about the limitations of his approach. Even converting every targeted lawn would represent less than one percent of U.S. land, he acknowledges. Critics argue that such a change cannot solve biodiversity loss on its own. “I never said Homegrown National Park is going to solve the biodiversity crisis,” he says. “Getting everybody involved and changing the culture is going to help. It’s going to help a lot.”
A recent feature in the New York Times questioned whether his insistence on native plants is out of date because some species adapt to a changing habitat. But Tallamy has shown in dozens of studies that native plants are crucial for many species’ survival.
The real metric, he argues, isn’t simply acreage restored but whether ecological thinking becomes mainstream. Evidence of that cultural shift, he believes, is already emerging. Demand for native plants now exceeds supply in many regions. Conservation landscaping is beginning to increase property values rather than diminish them. Native plant professionals are increasingly booked months in advance.
Still, Tallamy admits the movement remains tiny relative to the challenge. Even counting the two million people who visit Homegrown National Park’s website annually, “That’s nothing compared to 340 million people in the U.S. we need to reach.”
Mostly, he wants people to stop thinking of conservation as something professionals do somewhere else. “The object is to get people to realize that they have agency over what happens on their little piece of the Earth,” he emphasizes. “And that it matters.”

title: In Queens, Immigrant Women Sew a Truer Atlas
content:
In Queens, Immigrant Women Sew a Truer Atlas
The largely undocumented Latin American women of New York’s “costureros,” or needlework circles, are creating a countermap to archive the stories of their lives.
This article is part of a series focusing on underrepresented craft histories, researched and written by the 2025 Craft Archive Fellows, and organized in collaboration with the Center for Craft.
How can we delve into the archives of the present? Is it possible to unveil and touch the documents that communities are creating today to record and remember their history, or does understanding only arise with the passage of time? When does an object become an archive?
For the past two years, I have been working with two immigrant-led costureros: circles of women from all over Latin America that gather to create textiles together. Located in different community centers in Northwestern Queens in New York City, these spaces have become a safe haven for many undocumented, working-class immigrants who are enduring racial profiling and persecution under the current immigration crackdown. Amid this terror, the intimacy and secrecy of the costurero set a table where gossip and generosity sit side by side with threads and needles.
The first group, BordeAndo, was founded in 2018 as a community engagement initiative of the Queens Museum, though it soon grew beyond the institution to become an independent collective. Its name plays with multiple meanings in Spanish: bordar (to embroider), borde (border or frontier), and the suffix -ando, which evokes movement or walking. Most of its members come from the Ecuadorian highlands (la Sierra), though others are from the Dominican Republic, El Salvador, and Mexico. They range in age from 30 to 83 and have lived in the United States for between 10 and 50 years.
Las Comadres Bordadoras was founded in 2021 in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic by two Mexican immigrants, who sought to bring women out of isolation and foster a mutual support network. Their name, also difficult to translate, gestures toward camaraderie and kinship. The comadre refers specifically to women who are, in their words, “a midpoint between friend and family.” The comadres come from Mexico, Cuba, El Salvador, Uruguay, Colombia, Ecuador, and Argentina; range in age from 35 to 75; and have lived in the United States for between two and 30 years. They mostly embroider Mexican cloth napkins, but all forms of needlework are welcome. This costurero calls itself “nomadic” because it has moved around community gardens, public libraries, and schools in the area since its conception. Both circles are intergenerational, international spaces of confluence for transnational, working-class, largely undocumented immigrant women.
Last year, BordeAndo and Las Comadres Bordadoras were the protagonists of Thread of Voice / Un hilo de voz at the Queens Museum. The exhibition, which I curated, featured Andrés Altamirano’s photographs of the costurero members along with film by documentarian Eleonora Privitera. The visual narrative and documentation of this project was also done in collaboration with Altamirano.
I see these costureros as living archives — as sites where craft traditions converge, and concrete embodied and material practices connect geographies of affect and displacement, like a woman knitting a stitch learned by her grandmother back home or another embroidering a napkin for the altar of a dead loved one whose grave she cannot visit because of her migratory status. “Text” and “textile” share an etymological root — the Latin verb texere — that reveals both that texts are woven and textiles written. In this sense, textiles are texts that we have forgotten how to read, encoded with bodily gestures, storytelling practices, and materialities that could, if safeguarded, be called archives.

title: At 4, he lost his NYPD father on 9/11; 25 years later, he wears his badge
content:
At four years of age, Casey Kloepfer was too young to understand why his father never came home from work. Twenty-five years later, he carries that loss into the same department his father served, wearing his father's badge number and playing for the NYPD lacrosse team his father helped create, states an online report by NYC Government website. For Casey, the connection to his father is not confined to a photograph, a memorial or a family story. It is woven into the uniform he wears and the department he chose to join.
A father lost on September 11
Ronnie Kloepfer was an NYPD officer who was killed in the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. He was among the thousands of first responders who rushed toward danger as others tried to escape. His death left behind a family that, like so many others, had to navigate life without someone who had been at its center. Ronnie's connection to the NYPD extended beyond his work as a police officer. He was also instrumental in establishing the department's lacrosse team, bringing together officers through a sport he loved and the team would eventually become an unexpected bridge between generations.
Following his father's path
A quarter-century after September 11, Casey became an NYPD officer himself. His decision gave a new meaning to a legacy that could easily have remained rooted in the past.
He now wears his father's badge number, carrying a small but deeply personal reminder of the man whose career ended before Casey was old enough to understand it.
Casey is also part of the same lacrosse tradition his father helped establish. Alongside other officers whose families share similar connections to the department, he keeps alive something that began long before the attacks. The significance is particularly powerful because the NYPD's relationship with September 11 did not end when the World Trade Center towers fell. Hundreds of officers who responded that day and worked at Ground Zero in the months that followed have since died from illnesses linked to their service.
A legacy that keeps moving forward
The story of Casey and his father reflects a larger reality within the NYPD. The department has spent 25 years carrying the memory of those it lost while welcoming new generations who were children, or not yet born, when the attacks happened. For younger officers, September 11 can feel like distant history. For families such as the Kloepfers, it remains personal. Casey's uniform, badge number and place on his father's lacrosse team bring those two eras together. Ronnie's life was cut short on September 11, but the things he built did not disappear with him. His son now serves in the department he once served, and the lacrosse team he helped found continues to bring NYPD officers together.

title: Displaced by typhoons, Taiwan’s Bunun Indigenous people struggle to preserve heritage
content:
Wild grass now grows around the abandoned wooden houses of Tengjhih, a high-mountain hamlet in southern Taiwan, once a key settlement of the Bunun Indigenous people. Now, little remains except for the memories it holds.
Around 150 Bunun Indigenous residents of Tengjhih were permanently resettled in lowland areas after the deadly Typhoon Morakot in 2009 destroyed the only access road to their village, contributor Aylin Ho reports for Mongabay.
Typhoon Morakot killed 755 people across Taiwan, triggering catastrophic floods and landslides. While Indigenous peoples represented just 2.1% of Taiwan’s population at the time, approximately 70% of the land declared unsafe by authorities was located within Indigenous territories.
Efforts to rebuild the road to Tengjhih in 2012, 2021 and 2023 faced setbacks due to climate change-amplified rainfall and landslides. More recently, a typhoon in 2025 also devastated one section of the mountain, Ho reports. The indefinite closure of the surrounding Tengjhih National Forest Recreation Area has wiped out the local ecotourism and agricultural economy.
“When a major typhoon hits us, I have no income for the entire year,” said Bi’ Ismahasan, 70, a tea and coffee farmer who now relies on government assistance. “In 2026, I lost my entire harvest. Every year is worse than the previous one.”
Displacement has severed connections to ancestral land, threatening the transmission of cultural practices and language to younger generations.
“Today, when [young people] come back, there is no village and no work,” said Saminat Maliklan, 55, a Bunun cultural guide and one of five residents remaining in Tengjhih. “They have to adapt to an unfamiliar environment, and their ties with elders gradually fade. Our rituals and ceremonies are disappearing.”
The Taiwanese government’s resettlement program has drawn sharp criticism. Under the program, displaced families received ownership of lowland apartments but not the land beneath them, preventing residents from selling, expanding, or rebuilding their homes, according to news reports.
Tunkan Tansikian, a Bunun Indigenous rights and policy scholar at National Dong Hwa University, highlighted that relocation occurred without prior consultation, violating Taiwan’s 2005 Indigenous Peoples Basic Law.
“The purpose of the resettlement program was to persuade residents to abandon their mountain villages, which were considered dangerous, to reduce safety risks,” Tunkan said. “For Indigenous peoples, however, land is a core part of their culture, rather than being treated as a tradable and easily relinquished commodity.”
While local officials at the Taoyuan District Office have ruled out permanent resettlement due to landslide risks, an alternative access road is scheduled to open in January 2027 thanks to years of campaigning by Dahu Ismahasan, president of the Bunun tribal council.
“We still have hope … One day, the road will be better, and the lives of the people here will be better too,” Dahu said.

title: Jóvenes indígenas k’iche’ interpretan el clima para salvar cultivos en Guatemala
content:
- Comunidades indígenas k’iche’ de Totonicapán, en Guatemala, combinan monitoreo climático y saberes ancestrales para adaptarse a heladas, sequías y cambios extremos de temperatura.
- La información climática compartida a través de audios, mensajes y redes sociales permite que las familias campesinas tomen decisiones que evitan pérdidas agrícolas.
- La iniciativa es parte de un proyecto mayor que incluye estaciones meteorológicas, viveros agroforestales y la conservación de los bosques y fuentes de agua en otros departamentos de Guatemala.
- En 2026, los indígenas k’iche’ de Totonicapán sembraron 500 árboles y planean plantar 2000 más en los bosques de siete comunidades.
Antonela Huinac recuerda las historias que su papá narraba sobre la vida en Tacajalve, una aldea de San Francisco El Alto, municipio del departamento de Totonicapán. “Él nos contaba que, entre 1985 y 1995, la comunidad no sufría mucho calor. No había plagas, todo era muy ‘natural’”, dice.
Pensar en calor parecía una utopía en Totonicapán pues se ubica en el altiplano, en el occidente de Guatemala, e históricamente los informes del Instituto Nacional de Sismología, Vulcanología, Meteorología e Hidrología (Insivumeh) lo identifican como la región con las temperaturas más bajas del país, donde su población, en su mayoría indígena k’iche’, vive de la agricultura, especialmente de granos como el maíz y el frijol.
Sus habitantes aseguran que cosechaban bastante durante el invierno, tanto que podían almacenar una porción para consumir en verano, cuando no había cosechas porque éstas dependían del ciclo de la lluvia.
Pero todo eso cambió. Desde hace unos diez años, estima la gente en Tacajalve, el clima ya no es el mismo. “Dicen que esta es tierra fría, pero ya no”, lamenta la joven lideresa comunitaria, Antonela Huinac. “A estas alturas de mayo [hace diez años] ya estaba lloviendo, pero vemos que el clima hoy en día es de mucho calor”, agrega. En tiempos de crisis climática no solo el calor se vuelve extremo, el frío también.
La aparición más frecuente e incierta de otros fenómenos como las heladas es una grave amenaza cuando la subsistencia está basada en la agricultura. Cuando la temperatura desciende tanto y de manera imprevista, puede acabar con cultivos enteros en las comunidades.
Es por eso que un grupo de 25 jóvenes, entre ellos 18 mujeres, se han convertido en promotores climáticos que comparten la información que se obtiene en las estaciones meteorológicas de la Asociación de Cooperación para el Desarrollo Rural de Occidente (CDRO). Los jóvenes interpretan los datos y generan boletines para las comunidades de Tacajalve, Chivarreto, Chuicruz, Chuipachec, Xejuyup, Juchanep y Paxtocá. Equipados con anemómetros y veletas, estos jóvenes interpretan información climática y la convierten en mensajes que ya han salvado cultivos de las heladas.
Monitorear un clima cambiante
A unos treinta kilómetros de Tacajalve se encuentra el Sendero Ecológico El Aprisco, un parque natural privado ubicado en las montañas de Totonicapán y manejado por CDRO —organización de base comunitaria que, desde hace 40 años, ha coordinado proyectos que buscan mejorar las condiciones de vida de más de 132 comunidades en el occidente de Guatemala—. Este refugio natural se utiliza como un espacio de sensibilización y educación ambiental para quienes lo visitan, especialmente niños y niñas.
El Aprisco es un bosque de 13 hectáreas conformado principalmente por pinos y cedros. La presencia de esta vegetación brinda una sensación de frescura, muy distinta a la de San Francisco El Alto y la cabecera municipal de Totonicapán. Durante el invierno, los trabajadores deben utilizar chaquetas que los protejan del frío, que ha alcanzado los -5 °C.
El parque está conformado por una serie de senderos. Al final de uno de ellos, y a un lado de la carretera, se encuentra una especie de jaula que protege un artefacto metálico con varios elementos que sobresalen, entre los cuales está un tubo de unos tres metros de alto y apenas unos 20 centímetros de diámetro. Se encuentra en un área libre y lejos de los árboles.
“Conozca de meteorología: las estaciones meteorológicas permiten predecir y analizar las condiciones meteorológicas y de los fenómenos atmosféricos como ciclones, huracanes, tormentas y sequía”, se lee en un cártel ubicado en la entrada.
Los objetos que sobresalen son un anemómetro, un objeto con tres medias esferas que giran y miden la velocidad del viento, y una veleta, una especie de flecha metálica que indica su dirección. No puede verse desde la superficie, pero debajo de la tierra hay un pluviómetro que registra la cantidad de lluvia que cae y permite determinar cuánta agua y humedad hay debajo de la tierra.
CDRO instaló esta estación meteorológica en 2018 como una herramienta para que los productores agrícolas puedan conocer los futuros eventos climáticos y prepararse para responder ante ellos. Es una de las cuatro que la organización tiene en el departamento de Totonicapán, a las que recientemente sumó otras cuatro en el área entre Cunén y Santa Cruz del Quiché, en el departamento de Quiché.
Alan Pérez, técnico de CDRO encargado del monitoreo climático, detalla que la estación del Sendero Ecológico El Aprisco “recolecta datos del ambiente para tener información más clara sobre los sucesos meteorológicos que pueden ocurrir en esa área”.
Luego, CDRO entrega estos datos a los promotores climáticos que han sido formados para interpretarlos. Con base en los hallazgos, ellos generan boletines con recomendaciones agrícolas y forestales.
El principal objetivo es que la información llegue a la mayor cantidad de personas. Algunos boletines se publican en redes sociales, como grupos de Facebook, se envían por mensajes de Whatsapp e incluso por mensajes de texto. Otros, con el permiso de los líderes comunitarios, se pegan en lugares clave de las comunidades como los centros de salud. Con apoyo de profesionales de radio, también se han realizado 33 spots en lenguas Ki’che’ y Kaqchikel. Todo esto ha permitido que la población tome decisiones informadas.
En una ocasión, los promotores climáticos lograron informar a una vecina de Santa María Chiquimula —otro municipio de Totonicapán— de la llegada de una helada la mañana siguiente. Que la información llegara a la mujer, productora de hortalizas, representó toda una hazaña, pero demostró que el esfuerzo por divulgar la información valía la pena.
La mujer no tenía un teléfono inteligente y era analfabeta, así que no tenía manera de leer la información en redes sociales o por WhatsApp. Los monitores tuvieron que recurrir al envío a través de SMS a la hija de la agricultora para que le leyera el mensaje y le diera las indicaciones: debía regar la plantación en la noche o en la madrugada y utilizar tapescos (tejidos planos hechos con caña) para cubrirla.
Y así lo hicieron. El brócoli y la coliflor sobrevivieron mientras las mismas hortalizas de su vecina —que no se enteró de la helada— se perdieron. “Esta es una experiencia que nos ha motivado a seguir trabajando porque sí es de utilidad. Es una cosa tan sencilla, pero que le cambia la vida a una familia”, asegura Antonia Xuyup, directora del Sistema Ambiental Comunitario de CDRO.
Entre certezas e incertidumbres
Aunque el monitoreo climático no puede predecir con certeza la llegada de una helada con muchos días de anticipación, sí permitió que los jóvenes identificaran la prevalencia de condiciones que podían favorecerlas. Monitorearon las temperaturas mínimas diarias, la entrada de masas de aire frío (generalmente del norte), la humedad, la nubosidad y el viento.
“Las noches despejadas y con poco o ningún viento favorecen una mayor pérdida de calor del suelo, por lo que, si además se esperan temperaturas cercanas o por debajo de 0 °C, aumenta el riesgo de helada durante la madrugada o al amanecer del día siguiente”, explica Xuyup.
Durante el último invierno —entre noviembre de 2025 y enero de 2026—, la aldea de Tacajalve enfrentó no solo una sino varias heladas fuertes. En las noches, la temperatura disminuyó y osciló entre los 4 y 6 °C.
Las mujeres del grupo de jóvenes promotores establecieron una rutina para responder a este fenómeno. Cada noche colocaban cobijas y chamarras para proteger las semillas de aliso que apenas germinaban. La hora en la que lo hacían dependía de su propia percepción de la temperatura del ambiente. En los días muy fríos lo hacían desde las seis de la tarde y, en los días que eran un poco más frescos, las cubrían después de la medianoche.
Las jóvenes volvían al invernadero a las 5 o 6 de la mañana del siguiente día y debían retirar las chamarras para que los rayos de sol alcanzaran a las semillas. De esta manera, garantizaron que las plantas experimentaran un desarrollo normal.
“Las comunidades pueden tirar rastrojo para cubrir las raíces de las plantas para que no mueran ni se pierda el cultivo”, resume Pérez.
Por su parte, Antonela Huinac reconoce que las heladas de hace unos meses fueron un gran reto para ellos, “pero las plantas se cuidaron de la mejor manera porque nos adaptamos”, celebra.
Aún con todos los logros que han tenido, los jóvenes promotores y los profesionales de CDRO tienen algo claro: el monitoreo climático no reemplaza los saberes ni el conocimiento ancestral de la población k’iche’. Más bien, se complementan. Es por eso que los boletines también incluyen datos relacionados a la fase lunar en la que se encuentran. Según una tesis de la Universidad del Valle de Guatemala (UVG), se observó que al cosechar durante la luna llena los granos presentan menos humedad y por lo tanto menor número de insectos y menor daño durante el almacenamiento.
“Esto es fundamental porque los abuelos y abuelas saben que no en cualquier momento se puede sembrar un árbol”, explica Xuyup.
Reforestación: una herramienta para enfrentar el cambio del clima
La historia del grupo de promotores climáticos empezó en 2024 con el verde de los árboles. Al notar que la temperatura y la sensación térmica aumentaban en Tacajalve, Antonela Huinac, junto a la pastoral juvenil de la iglesia católica a la que asiste, decidió unirse a una jornada de reforestación en San Antonio Sija, otra aldea de San Francisco El Alto.
El Grupo Intergubernamental de Expertos sobre el Cambio Climático (IPCC, por sus siglas en inglés), en su informe global de 2022, ya indicaba que la protección y restauración de bosques puede moderar el calor local mediante sombra y evapotranspiración. En ciudades, la evidencia sintetizada por el IPCC señala que aumentar la vegetación reduce el calor y los extremos térmicos, mientras que en áreas rurales también hay beneficios microclimáticos, pero se intersectan con otras variables como el tipo de paisaje y el agua disponible.
Aunque la ciencia ya había hablado de esto, en Tacajalve se dieron cuenta que los árboles jugaban un papel central en la ecuación climática acudiendo al dato empírico. En la zona donde la carretera atraviesa la comunidad, el sol pega con fuerza y “se siente la diferencia porque allí no hay árboles que refresquen”, dice Huinac. Ella y sus jóvenes compañeros empezaron a preguntarse: “¿Cómo podemos ayudar a nuestra madre tierra, a nuestra naturaleza?”.
Decidieron pasar de las palabras a la acción, buscaron posibles donantes de árboles y fue así como dieron con CDRO.
En mayo de 2024, la organización les dio 150 cipreses (Cupressus) y 150 árboles de pino blanco (Pinus chiapensis), especies nativas en Guatemala. Realizaron la jornada de siembra el día 24 de ese mes. CDRO también les impartió talleres sobre reforestación y el cuidado de ciertas especies de plantas.
Al finalizar el proceso y luego de ver el interés de los jóvenes, CDRO les ofreció instalar un vivero en su aldea. Ellos aceptaron y consiguieron un terreno —que la familia de Antonela Huinac prestó— donde construyeron esa “sala cuna de árboles”. En especial las mujeres del grupo se encargaron, con palas y picos, de nivelar el suelo que se ubicaba en una pendiente y, actualmente, son quienes garantizan el cuidado de las semillas y plántulas que posteriormente se convierten en árboles para reforestar.
En 2026, ellas y grupos organizados de la comunidad, como los comités de agua potable, ya han sembrado 500 plántulas de aliso (Alnus acuminata) que fueron cuidadas en el vivero. Además, junto con las autoridades comunitarias, han planificado plantar 2000 más a partir de septiembre, cuando esperan que llegue la lluvia.
Huinac ha asumido el liderazgo de la iniciativa de reforestación y motiva a sus compañeras a seguir en el proceso, al tiempo que trabaja desde su casa en el oficio de corte y confección de ropa.
La información climática no debería ser un lujo
Raquel Sigüenza, representante de la Unión Internacional para la Conservación de la Naturaleza (UICN) en Guatemala, considera que el monitoreo climático reduce la vulnerabilidad de las comunidades al sustituir la incertidumbre por información climática local y oportuna. Esto permite, según la experta, que las inversiones sean sostenibles a los efectos extremos del cambio climático. Es por eso que la organización internacional, a través de su proyecto Altiplano Resiliente, apoya la labor de CDRO con sus estaciones de monitoreo meteorológico.
“El enfoque de la UICN no se centra sólo en establecer sistemas de monitoreo que arrojen datos técnicos, también se enfoca en asegurar que esa información llegue a actores locales para quienes históricamente la información climática no es accesible, ayudando de esta manera a reducir la brecha de acceso a la información climática. Es una forma de justicia climática”, explica Sigüenza. “La información climática ya no es un lujo al alcance de pocos”.
La UICN no solo apoya en Guatemala a la iniciativa de monitoreo climático de CDRO y los jóvenes promotores. También acompaña otros proyectos relacionados con la adaptación de prácticas agroforestales con las que han llegado a 132 000 personas pertenecientes a los pueblos indígenas k’iche’, Kaqchikel y Mam. Especialmente a mujeres, jóvenes y hogares monoparentales femeninos.
En medio de los esfuerzos, Sigüenza reconoce que el monitoreo climático ha enfrentado dificultades en la región. Las principales están relacionadas con capacidades técnicas y operativas limitadas en los municipios y organizaciones comunitarias, barreras culturales reflejadas en resistencia a nuevas prácticas de restauración y brechas de género.
Las dificultades mencionadas por Sigüenza se viven también a escala mundial. Actualmente, la gran mayoría de las redes comunitarias operan gracias a asignaciones temporales de fondos de la cooperación internacional o proyectos de ONG que, al expirar, dejan a las comunidades sin presupuesto para reponer equipos dañados, comprar sensores o mantener activas las plataformas de comunicación.
Además, en cuanto a brecha de género, según datos de la Organización de las Naciones Unidas para la Alimentación y la Agricultura (FAO, por sus siglas en inglés), si las mujeres agricultoras tuvieran el mismo acceso que los hombres a recursos productivos, sus rendimientos podrían aumentar entre 20 % y 30 %.
Aún así, tanto UICN como CDRO y los jóvenes promotores consideran que el monitoreo climático es una iniciativa que debe continuar porque sí ha tenido un impacto positivo en reducir la pérdida de cosechas. “Vale la pena porque con este tipo de pérdidas las familias quedan muy dañadas, no solo en la parte productiva, sino emocional y psicológica”, finaliza Xuyup.
*Este reportaje es una alianza periodística entre Agencia Ocote y Mongabay Latam.

title: Recuperación de la capa de ozono: ¿Qué dice el último informe de las Naciones Unidas?
content:
En el marco de la conmemoración, hoy 16 de septiembre, del Día de la Capa de Ozono, la Organización de las Naciones Unidas (ONU) saludó los avances alcanzados en la recuperación de esa zona de la estratosfera terrestre; entre ellos la eliminación del 99 % de las sustancias químicas que la afectan.


Se indica al respecto que ello deriva de los esfuerzos efectuados a nivel mundial en base a lo establecido en el Protocolo de Montreal.
“La cooperación internacional puede dar resultados ante los grandes desafíos ambientales”, señala el organismo multilateral desde sus redes sociales.
El Protocolo de Montreal fue firmado el 16 de septiembre de 1987; razón por la cual se celebra en esa fecha el Día de la Capa de Ozono.
El documento establecía acuerdos respecto al tratamiento de las sustancias que agotan a la capa de ozono, parte de la atmósfera que protege a todos los seres vivientes y a sus ecosistemas de los efectos de la radiación ultravioleta excesiva.
Resultados concretos
Como resultado de este consenso, se han eliminado casi el 99 % de las sustancias que agotan la capa de ozono, con lo cual esta capa protectora viene reponiéndose.
Sin capa de ozono, la proliferación de enfermedades como el cáncer de piel y cataratas sería muchísimo mayor a la actual, así como el deterioro de plantas y cultivos y de la calidad de vida de humanos y animales.
"El Protocolo de Montreal es uno de los mejores ejemplos que tenemos del resultado positivo y poderoso del multilateralismo", señaló al respecto Meg Seki, secretaria ejecutiva de la Secretaría del Ozono del Programa de las Naciones Unidas para el Medio Ambiente.

Dicho instrumento ha establecido parámetros para atenuar los problemas del clima, la biodiversidad y la contaminación, apuntó.
Destacó, por tanto, que "cuando la ciencia sólida es la base para la acción universal, podemos superar los desafíos ambientales que nos parezcan insuperables", añadió Seki.
Seki recordó, en ese sentido, que fueron científicos los que a mediados de la década de 1970 establecieron que elementos químicos incluidos en productos de uso cotidiano, como aerosoles, equipos de aire acondicionado, refrigeradores y otros, dañaban a la capa de ozono.
Agujero en la Antártida
1985 marcó otro punto de inflexión, al comprobarse en aquel año que existía un agujero en la capa de ozono situada sobre la Antártida. Ello derivó en la adopción del Convenio de Viena para la protección de esta capa, firmado en aquel año.
Con los resultados positivos que derivan de las medidas adoptadas mundialmente, se espera que para la década de 2060 el referido agujero se cierre.
En dicho documento —cuyos alcances empezaron a entrar en vigor en 1989 y que es el primer acuerdo de la ONU ratificado por todos los países del mundo— se estableció la prohibición gradual de sustancias como los clorofluorocarbonos (CFC), que debilitan a la capa de ozono.
Sin las medidas que se adoptaron en base al Protocolo de Montreal, las plantas, la vegetación y el suelo habrían sido menos capaces de almacenar carbono, derivando ello en un aumento de la temperatura global de entre 0,5 °C y 1,0 °C.

title: Recicla gran parte de su ropa y le pone detalles indígenas, dice la Presidenta
content:
Orgullosa de sus raíces, no recurre a grandes diseñadores ni gasta tanto, aclara
Viernes 18 de septiembre de 2026, p. 5
La presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo reveló que gran parte de la ropa que habitualmente usa la “recicla”, además de que sobre las prendas, expertos en costura colocan piezas artesanales, como bordados o huipiles.
Al aludir ayer al vestido que usó en la ceremonia del Grito de Independencia, el día 15, que fue bordado por artesanas muxes del Istmo de Tehuantepec, la mandataria aclaró que no hace grandes gastos en su indumentaria.
Señaló que no opta por ropa de diseñadores internacionales, sino que prefiere piezas más tradicionales y de origen artesanal.
“Tampoco es que estemos gastando quién sabe cuánto para tener una ropa distinta cada vez.”
Apuntó que hay interrogantes sobre la cantidad de vestimenta que tendría, ante lo que aclaró que con apoyo de una costurera que colabora con ella, se hacen ajustes a las mismas piezas.
“¿De dónde saco yo este bordado? La gran mayoría son regalos que me hace la gente cuando voy a distintos lugares. Me regalan un rebozo, un huipil, algún textil. Entonces, tomamos una partecita y lo reciclamos en los trajes.
“¿Por qué uso esta ropa? ¿Por qué me importa? Porque no hay nada más hermoso que esto, que son artesanas y artesanos mexicanos, y que viene de hace mucho. Ahora, los bordados tehuanos de Oaxaca, pues es una identidad. Oaxaca tiene una diversidad enorme de textiles y cada uno representa algo distinto.
“¿Por qué no usar una alta costura de un francés o de algún otro país y por qué usar lo nuestro? Pues porque es nuestra identidad y hay que tener orgullo por ello.”
A pregunta en la mañanera de por qué no mencionó a Ignacio Allende en sus arengas del Grito, la mandataria aclaró que no fue un olvido, sino que deseaba dar relevancia a figuras que no son tan recordadas, como Guadalupe Victoria, quien junto con Vicente Guerrero mantuvo “la llama de la Independencia tras el fusilamiento de Morelos”.

title: Sharpeville massacre, 66 years on: Families still wait for justice
content:
Sharpeville massacre, 66 years on: Families still wait for justice
More than six decades after police opened fire on protesters, survivors and relatives are taking their fight to court.
Sharpeville, South Africa – Paulina Mathinye was five years old when her father left home for a meeting near the police station in Sharpeville, a township south of Johannesburg.
She remembers waiting for him to return.
“I’ll go run to him,” Mathinye recalled thinking. “He will pick me up like daddies always do with their beloved daughters.”
He never did.
On March 21, 1960, Mathinye’s father joined other men from the community at a gathering protesting apartheid’s pass laws, which required Black South Africans to carry documents restricting where they could live and work.
“There was a meeting here at the old police station, so he accompanies those fathers to the meeting. But then he never came back.”
Police opened fire on the protesters that day in what became known as the Sharpeville Massacre.
Apartheid-era police records put the death toll at 69 and the number of injured at 180. Research published in 2024 using police records found that as many as 91 people may have been killed and 238 injured. The higher figures are also cited by lawyers representing Sharpeville survivors and families.
The massacre became a defining moment in South Africa’s struggle against apartheid. March 21 is now commemorated as Human Rights Day, and South Africa’s democratic Constitution was signed in Sharpeville in 1996.
But for the families of those killed and injured, the consequences did not end that day.
More than six decades later, survivors and relatives are seeking redress through the courts.
Lawyers for Human Rights has filed an application in the Gauteng High Court challenging the continued existence of the Indemnity Act 61 of 1961, an apartheid-era law that the applicants say prevented survivors and dependants of those killed from pursuing civil and criminal proceedings arising from the massacre.
The applicants are also seeking certification of a class action involving survivors who were shot and dependants of those killed.
For Mathinye, the legal fight is inseparable from the life that followed her father’s death.
He had been the family’s breadwinner. After he was killed, her mother worked as a domestic worker to support five children.
“We sometimes go to bed with empty stomach. We sometimes go to school and when we come back from school we find nothing to eat.”
There was no electricity, and sometimes her mother could not afford even a candle for the children to study.
“There was no light. There was no library. Struggle even to buy a candle, a mere candle.”
Mathinye wanted to become a teacher.
She stayed in school and applied to study further, but her family could not afford it. She eventually began working while still young to help support her mother and siblings.
When she encounters people she went to school with who became teachers and nurses, she thinks about the life she might have had.
“If my father was not shot, maybe I was going to be one of those people… Maybe by this time I would be a teacher.”
Why now?
The effort to seek redress is not new.
Charne Tracey-Mamdoo, a lawyer in the Strategic Litigation Programme at Lawyers for Human Rights, told Al Jazeera that victims and families attempted to pursue claims soon after the massacre.
“Immediately after the Sharpeville massacre, victims and families did attempt to pursue these sorts of claims, but they were barred because in 1961 the apartheid government enacted the Indemnity Act.”
The applicants argue that the Act created a legal barrier to civil and criminal proceedings arising from conduct covered by the legislation.
The current case challenges that barrier.
Lawyers for Human Rights is asking the High Court to declare the Indemnity Act unconstitutional and invalid. It is also seeking certification of a class action for survivors who were shot and dependants of those killed.
The applicants must first persuade the court to grant the constitutional relief they seek and certify the proposed class action. If the case proceeds, individual claims for damages could then be pursued.
More than 70 survivors and relatives have expressed support for or interest in the proposed litigation, according to Lawyers for Human Rights.
Tracey-Mamdoo said lawyers had spent years locating surviving victims and witnesses, reconstructing claims and gathering historical and expert evidence.
The survivors’ age has added urgency. Many of those directly affected by the massacre are now elderly, and some who spent decades seeking redress have died without seeing the matter resolved.
An inheritance of loss
Ishmael Poho was six years old when his father left home for a community meeting on March 21.
Poho wanted to go with him.
“He said, ‘No, I’ll come back. You need to stay home.’”
Poho saw his father again briefly that day.
“That was the last time I saw my father that day.”
It took his mother three days to find his body.
According to Poho’s account, related partly through an interpreter, his mother searched police stations before eventually finding him among bodies that had been placed in garages.
“At that station, there were vehicle garages as part of the building and the infrastructure. However, bodies were piled up or stacked up in those garages,” the interpreter said.
His father’s death changed the family’s circumstances.
His mother had never worked and did not speak English. She eventually found work as a domestic worker in a nearby white neighbourhood. As the children grew older, they also worked to support the household.
Poho, now 72, thinks about the people he went to school with who became teachers, nurses and other health professionals.
“If my father was alive, I would have been different. My life would have been different from the life I have lived.”
For Mauleen Maine, the loss began before she was born.
Her uncle was 23 when he was killed.
According to family history passed down by her grandmother, he had returned from a night shift, gone to buy bread and then returned to the meeting.
He had been the family’s breadwinner.
After his death, Maine’s grandmother struggled financially and eventually sold liquor to survive. She died without seeing the matter resolved.
Maine’s parents later continued seeking redress. They too died without seeing justice.
Now Maine, 62, is continuing the effort.
She told Al Jazeera through an interpreter that compensation alone would not be enough. Her family also wants better housing and educational opportunities for their children.
For families like hers, the question is not only what was lost in 1960, but what might have been different in the decades that followed.
What would justice mean?
For Vincent Thamae, a member of Voices of Sharpeville who has worked with survivors and families, the case cannot be reduced to compensation.
“It’s not a question of the amount of money. It’s the question of how much does it need for a change in the lives of the victims and survivors?”
Thamae argues that the effects of the massacre reached beyond those who were shot.
“The victims were not only those who were shot,” he said. “We maintain even the whole township was a victim.”
Lawyers for Human Rights says the plaintiffs also want dialogue with the South African government about appropriate reparations and recognition.
The formal court case, however, is narrower. The applicants are challenging the Indemnity Act and seeking relief that would enable the proposed class action to proceed. The court has not yet ruled that the Act is unconstitutional, nor has it determined that the government is liable to compensate the applicants.
That distinction matters because Sharpeville occupies a powerful place in South Africa’s democratic identity.
It is remembered every year as a symbol of the struggle for human rights.
For some of the families who lived through the massacre, however, remembrance has not amounted to redress.
Lawyers for Human Rights says 51 Sharpeville survivors were formally awarded reparations through the Truth and Reconciliation Commission process.
Poho had expected the democratic government to address the concerns of survivors and families.
“We were happy that a Black government had stepped into office, and we were hopeful that our issues would be met and, you know, justice realised, only to realise it became worse. Nothing ever came.”
The government respondents will have an opportunity to respond to the application before the High Court considers the relief sought.
There is no clear timetable for the proceedings.
For Tracey-Mamdoo, the age of the survivors makes the case urgent.
“They’ve already waited a very long time for this to happen and we are doing everything we can to just kind of move that process forward.”
Mathinye is now 71. Poho is 72.
Their fathers died more than six decades ago.
Their families have lived with the consequences ever since.
Children grew up without fathers. Breadwinners were lost. Educational opportunities disappeared. Mothers struggled to keep households afloat. And in some families, the next generation inherited not only the consequences of the massacre but also the fight for redress.
Sharpeville is remembered as a turning point in South Africa’s history.
For these families, the story remains unfinished.
And Mathinye is still asking the question she has carried since she was five.
“Why did they shoot my father?”

title: Senado aprova garantia do direito à natureza para crianças e adolescentes
content:
Senado aprova garantia do direito à natureza para crianças e adolescentes
Chamado de ECA Ambiental, proposta define como dever da família, da sociedade e do Estado a efetivação do contato com o meio natural
Chamado de ECA Ambiental, proposta define como dever da família, da sociedade e do Estado a efetivação do contato com o meio natural
Um projeto que estabelece princípios e diretrizes para garantir o direito da criança e do adolescente à natureza, “com absoluta prioridade”, foi aprovado no Senado na última quarta-feira (2). O PL 2.225/2024 da deputada federal Laura Carneiro (PSD-RJ) agora segue para sanção presidencial.
A proposta estabelece prioridade no recebimento de amparo em situações de riscos socioambientais e climáticos, além de assegurar “o acesso a áreas naturais saudáveis”, o “brincar livre” e a “educação baseada na natureza”. Terão prioridade na efetivação dessas garantias às crianças na primeira infância e aquelas com deficiência. De acordo com o texto, o atendimento pleno desse direito é objetivo a ser buscado pela União, estados, Distrito Federal e municípios.
Para consolidar essas diretrizes, o texto inclui o direito da infância ao meio ambiente equilibrado entre os princípios da Política Nacional do Meio Ambiente (Lei 6.938, de 1981). Além disso, o Estatuto da Criança e do Adolescente (ECA – Lei 8.069, de 1990) passa a definir como dever da família, da sociedade e do Estado a efetivação do contato com o meio natural. Por fim, a Política Nacional sobre Mudança do Clima (Lei 12.187, de 2009) ganha um dispositivo que torna obrigatória a atuação governamental prioritária na mitigação dos impactos climáticos sobre esse público.
Em sua justificativa, o senador Alessandro Vieira, relator do projeto, destaca as soluções baseadas na natureza esperadas. “Pátios naturalizados, arborização, sombreamento, permeabilidade do solo, manejo integrado das águas, uso de espécies nativas e integração com o território são medidas compatíveis com soluções baseadas na natureza e com políticas contemporâneas de resiliência urbana”, afirma.
A aprovação é resultado de uma construção conjunta entre parlamentares, organizações da sociedade civil, especialistas em crianças e adolescentes, que participaram da mobilização em torno da proposta desde o início de sua tramitação.
Para o Alana, organização em prol das crianças, a aprovação é um avanço importante para incorporar a proteção de crianças e adolescentes às políticas de prevenção, adaptação e resposta à crise climática no Brasil.
“O avanço do ECA Ambiental reforça a necessidade de colocar a infância no centro das decisões sobre o clima e abre caminho para que as políticas de adaptação climática passem a considerar, de forma mais concreta, as necessidades de crianças e adolescentes. É também um passo para preparar melhor escolas, cidades e territórios para uma realidade em que eventos extremos tendem a ser cada vez mais presentes”, diz Tayanne Galeno, coordenadora de Relações Governamentais do Alana.
A aprovação do ECA Ambiental ganha peso ainda maior diante das projeções para o super El Niño de 2026/2027. Os cenários climáticos alertam para chuvas acima da média no Sul durante o último trimestre de 2026, períodos de menor precipitação na Amazônia e em parte do Nordeste, além de temperaturas mais altas em grande parte do país. A combinação desses fatores pode aumentar o risco de incêndios florestais e a ocorrência de eventos extremos, com impactos especialmente graves para crianças e adolescentes.
“O trabalho, porém, não termina com a aprovação da lei: será preciso transformar o avanço no Congresso em políticas públicas capazes de responder aos impactos que crianças e adolescentes já enfrentam e aos que podem surgir nos próximos anos”, conclui Tayanne.

title: Lalbaugcha Raja: How a broken market and a vow created Mumbai’s iconic Ganpati
content:
Mumbai’s most famous Ganpati did not begin with a grand pandal or celebrity crowds. Its story began with a market that had shut down, families worried about their livelihood and a promise made to Lord Ganesha. In 1934, that promise took the form of an idol. More than nine decades later, Lalbaugcha Raja remains one of Mumbai’s most powerful symbols of faith and community.
When a market disappeared, so did livelihoods
In 1932, a market near Peru Chawl in Lalbaug was shut down. The closure affected vendors, traders and fishermen, including members of the local Koli community who depended on the area for their livelihood.
The community wanted a permanent marketplace. They prayed for a place where they could continue their trade. Their wish was eventually fulfilled when land was made available for a permanent market, which became the present Lalbaug Market.
A vow became Lalbaugcha Raja
The community’s gratitude became a religious promise, or navas. In September 1934, the traders and fishermen installed a public
Ganesha idol dressed in the traditional attire of a fisherman.
The Lalbaugcha Raja Sarvajanik Ganeshotsav Mandal was established in 1934. The idol soon became associated with the idea of a Navsacha Ganpati, or Ganesha believed to fulfil devotees’ wishes.
That origin gives the festival a meaning that goes beyond spectacle. At its heart is a very ordinary human hope: finding work, stability and a place to belong.
The Kambli family gave the Raja his familiar face
The idol’s distinctive form has another remarkable story. The Kambli family has been making the Lalbaugcha Raja idol since 1935, when Madhusudan Donduji Kambli began the tradition. Three generations of the family have since carried the work forward.
In 2011, Kambli Arts secured intellectual-property protection for the traditional design, after replicas of the famous idol became increasingly common.
So the Raja seen today is not simply a yearly sculpture. It carries a recognisable artistic tradition that has been carefully passed down.
Why millions still stand in line
The scale of Lalbaugcha Raja today is almost difficult to imagine. The idol is widely reported to attract around 1.5 million devotees a day during the festival.
There are separate arrangements for Mukh Darshan and Charan Sparsh or Navsachi darshan. Long queues, sometimes stretching for many hours, have become part of the Lalbaug experience.
The Maharashtra Tourism Department describes
Ganesh Chaturthi as a festival that brings together devotion, culture and community life. Lalbaugcha Raja is perhaps one of Mumbai’s clearest examples of that idea.
92 years completed, 93rd year begins
The mandal is celebrating its 93rd year in 2026, with the festival running from September 14 to September 25.
There is, however, one detail often missed in retellings of the story. The annual celebration was not literally held without interruption. In 2020, the mandal cancelled its traditional festivities during the COVID-19 pandemic and instead focused on awareness activities.
That interruption does not weaken the story. If anything, it makes the history more human. Lalbaugcha Raja began with people asking for a livelihood, survived generations of change and continues to bring strangers together every Ganesh Chaturthi.
Disclaimer: Historical accounts of Lalbaugcha Raja contain traditional narratives alongside documented records. Details such as the navas and its wish-fulfilling reputation reflect community belief and should not be treated as independently verifiable supernatural claims.

title: 25 Years After September 11th, New York City Changed the Way We Prepare for Disasters
content:
This post was originally published by the National Center for Disaster Preparedness.
Twenty-five years after September 11th, 2001, it is still difficult to contemplate what happened without first thinking about the people. The firefighters and police officers who ran toward the World Trade Center, the emergency managers and health professionals trying to make sense of an unconceivable situation, the transit workers helping people evacuate Lower Manhattan, and the countless New Yorkers who simply tried to help one another are part of the city’s history. For those of us who work in the disaster risk management sector, September 11th is also a marker in the history of how we prepare, respond, and recover. The attacks exposed serious weaknesses in information sharing and coordination, but they also demonstrated an aspect of equal importance: when a disaster overwhelms an entire system, disaster survivors and organizations need to find ways to collaborate that may not have existed before the disaster began.
One of the most distinct ways to understand how dramatically the field has changed is to consider the technical tools emergency managers had available to them in 2001. New York City was already using geographic information systems (GIS), and these digital maps became enormously valuable during the response and recovery. However, transferring large digital files across networked systems was constrained by limited bandwidth, slower network speeds, and substantially less mature data infrastructure than emergency responders have access to today. Internet capacity was so limited that critical GIS disk drives had to be delivered daily by state troopers from offices in Albany to New York City so they could be used in the response. There were no smartphones, no social media, and no cloud-based systems through which responders could immediately share information or communicate with the public. Today, satellite imagery, digital maps, mobile communications, real-time data and increasingly sophisticated analytical tools are so commonplace that it can be easy to forget how innovative and useful they would have seemed on September 11th.
The communications problems that morning were not simply a matter of having cumbersome technology tools. The destruction of infrastructure in Lower Manhattan, combined with the extraordinary volume of people trying to communicate, overwhelmed telephone, cellular, and radio systems. Responders lost contact with colleagues and leadership and, critically, did not always have the information they needed about what was happening inside the towers. In the middle of an emergency, information can be as critical as any physical resource, yet it only becomes useful when it can move between people and organizations. This lesson helped change emergency management for the better. Since September 11th, New York City and other jurisdictions have invested heavily in interoperable communications, emergency operations centers, GIS, mass notification, mutual aid, regional planning, and training programs that bring agencies together to practice before a disaster occurs. We have become much more aware that a major disaster in New York is never the responsibility of a single agency.
Perhaps the most important change, however, has been cultural. Emergency management has become much more focused on relationships among organizations and on the ability to adapt to emergent events. The people responding to September 11th were not unprepared; many were among the most highly trained public safety professionals in the U.S. Instead, they were confronting something for which there was no precedent. The lesson was not that planning had failed, but that no plan can anticipate every scenario. Good preparedness therefore means creating organizations that can recognize when their assumptions are wrong, share information quickly, request assistance, and adapt. Contemporary training exercises are most valuable when they expose those unnerving moments when a plan breaks down, and responders have to figure out together what to do next.
A new generation of leaders has also developed professionally in the years since September 11th. Many of today’s emergency managers, public safety officials, hospital managers and disaster researchers began their careers around that time or were shaped by its aftermath. They have subsequently dealt with hurricanes, floods, wildfires, pandemics, infrastructure failures and other emergencies that have reinforced the same primary lesson: disasters cross boundaries. A hospital may depend on the electric grid; a transit system may determine whether people can reach safety; a private company may control infrastructure essential to public response; and community organizations may know things that government agencies cannot fathom from an emergency operations center. The strongest response is therefore rarely about one institution having all the answers. It is about people knowing whom to call, trusting one another, and being willing to share what they know.
We should be proud of how far this evolution has taken us, but we should also be cautious to assume that progress means we are prepared for everything. That’s far from true. The U.S. remains vulnerable to unprecedented disasters that could overwhelm the systems we have built, and preparedness requires sustained attention even when the immediate crisis has passed. Changes in federal priorities, programs and policies can also create uncertainty for state, local, Tribal, and territorial emergency managers who are trying to plan years ahead. At the same time, technology is moving faster than many of our public institutions. Artificial intelligence, remote sensing, automated damage assessments and predictive modeling may dramatically improve our ability to understand a disaster as it unfolds, but such digital tools cannot replace leadership or trust. A sophisticated system is of limited value if the people who need to use it do not adequately communicate with one another.
Twenty-five years later, I think that is one of the most important lessons we should carry forward. We cannot know what the next catastrophic event will look like, and the technologies available to us in another 25 years may be difficult to imagine today. What we can do is continue learning from experience, investing in systems that let credible information flow freely, and developing leaders who know how to collaborate and build relationships before they are needed. The greatest homage to the people who responded on September 11th is not to just remember what they did that day. It is to use what we learned from their experience to make the next response more effective. New York City has spent 25 years doing exactly that, and the work is not finished.
Thomas Chandler is a senior research scientist and the director of the National Center for Disaster Preparedness.
