title: La tasa de analfabetismo en el país es la más baja en la historia
content:
La Unesco reconoce que 96% de los mexicanos saben leer y escribir
Miércoles 9 de septiembre de 2026, p. 9
San Juan Chamula, Chis., En el marco del Congreso Mundial por el 60 aniversario del Día Internacional de la Alfabetización 2026, la Organización de Naciones Unidas para la Educación, la Ciencia y la Cultura (Unesco) felicitó a México por sus progresos en materia de alfabetización, al ser un país que “avanza en esta materia”.
Lo anterior, luego de que el país alcanzara la tasa de analfabetismo más baja de su historia: del total de la población de 15 años y más, quienes no saben leer ni escribir representan 3.8 por ciento; es decir, más de 96 por ciento son alfabetizados.
Lidia Arthur Brito, subdirectora general de la Unesco, quien encabezó la ceremonia oficial en esta comunidad, en el corazón de los Altos de Chiapas, destacó la conducción de la presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo en dichos progresos.
“Quiero reconocer el liderazgo de la Presidenta, quien es la primera mujer en llegar a este cargo en México, y es además, una gran científica. Sabemos que ella, con todo su equipo, con todo el pueblo mexicano, continúan el sueño de Benito Juárez, de Justo Sierra, de José Vasconcelos, y claro, de Jaime Torres Bodet, el segundo director general de la Unesco, y dos veces titular de la Secretaría de Educación Pública, quienes ponen a México en la ruta de un país completamente alfabetizado”, afirmó en la Plaza de la Paz de esta comunidad, ante miles de indígenas de todas las etnias del estado.
Afirmó que los avances de nuestro país y, en particular, de comunidades indígenas como San Juan Chamula, “demuestra que la alfabetización no consiste únicamente en adquirir competencias de lectura y escritura, sino también en fortalecer la identidad, preservar las lenguas y ampliar las oportunidades de desarrollo para todas las personas”.
Chiapas, declaró, es un ejemplo de diversidad que distingue a México. Sus pueblos han mantenido vivas las tradiciones, conocimientos y formas de organización, que “constituyen un patrimonio invaluable para la humanidad”.
Acompañada del titular de la SEP, Mario Delgado Carrillo y del gobernador de Chiapas, Eduardo Ramírez Aguilar, Brito destacó que la educación “es más poderosa cuando dialoga con las culturas, las lenguas y los saberes”.
Antes de la entrega de los Premios Internacionales de Alfabetización Unesco 2026, que en esta edición reconocieron a seis proyectos innovadores en México, Líbano, Nigeria, Colombia, Países Bajos y Tailandia, entre ellos el Programa de Alfabetización Chiapas Puede, la subdirectora general de la Unesco admitió que, pese a los avances alcanzados en las décadas recientes, pues la tasa de jóvenes alfabetizados en el mundo pasó de 75 a 93 por ciento entre 1975 y 2024, “tenemos que reflexionar sobre lo que realmente significa la alfabetización en el siglo XXI”.
Admitió que la alfabetización “va más allá de la escritura y la lectura, porque abarca los conocimientos, las competencias y las capacidades necesarias para desenvolverse plenamente en la sociedades actuales, y navegar por un mundo muy complejo”.

title: People Of Purpose: How Prerana Founder Priti Patkar Reached 19,883 Children From Red-Light Areas Across Maharashtra
content:
For Priti Patkar, social work began not with a predetermined career path, but with a question that emerged from witnessing the lives of children growing up in Mumbai’s red-light areas: how could children born into exploitation be given the opportunity to choose a different future.
Trained as a social worker at Nirmala Niketan and later at the Tata Institute of Social Sciences, where she stood first in her specialisation, Priti’s understanding of child protection was shaped by her early exposure to Kamathipura. Her journey eventually led to the founding of Prerana, an organisation focused on protecting women and children from trafficking, commercial sexual exploitation and other forms of violence.
A Defining Encounter With Kamathipura
A visit to Kamathipura in 1986 became a turning point in Priti’s life. As a social-work student, she encountered children growing up amid circumstances where exploitation could continue across generations.
What stayed with her was three generations and the youngest of them being a child of women from the same family on the streets and bylanes of Kamathipura, soliciting for customers. The experience made her confront a difficult question: what could be done to ensure that children born into such circumstances were not automatically destined to inherit the same life?
At the time, children’s rights were receiving increasing attention globally, yet Priti saw how children in places like Kamathipura remained largely invisible while many of their basic rights were being violated.
That experience became part of the foundation for Prerana, which she began with her husband, Dr. Pravin Patkar, with support and guidance from Mrs. Farida Lambay and Dr. Hazel D’Lima.
From Rescue To Prevention
Priti’s early experiences also changed how she understood social intervention. She realised that protecting children could not simply mean removing them from immediate danger.
Children needed safe spaces, education, healthcare, counselling, family support and pathways towards a different future. This thinking led to the development of Prerana’s Night Care Centre programme, described in the interview as the first initiative of its kind.
The programme provided children born to women in prostitution with a safe place to stay during the night, away from the violence, exploitation and influences of the red-light area. But the intervention went beyond shelter. Children were supported with education, healthcare, nutrition and psychosocial care.
Prerana also worked with their mothers. The intention was not to separate mothers and children, but to protect children while recognising the importance of their relationships with their families.
For Priti, that distinction remains central. The goal was never to decide what a child should become. It was to create the conditions in which a child could eventually decide for themselves.
Challenging Stigma And Intergenerational Trafficking
The work was not without resistance. Priti recalls that there was widespread stigma surrounding children born to women in prostitution, including the assumption that they would inevitably enter the same trade as their mothers.
Prerana had to challenge both the circumstances surrounding these children and the assumptions society had made about their futures.
The organisation also encountered resistance from people benefiting from the sex trade, particularly when children were supported in making choices that could take them away from exploitation. Priti emphasises that rescue alone cannot protect a child from being trafficked again. Without safe environments, education, family and community support, rehabilitation and continued services, children can remain vulnerable to re-trafficking.
Its work with women similarly extended beyond immediate assistance. Prerana has supported access to alternative rehabilitation and livelihood opportunities, social-security entitlements, identity and protection documents, and government schemes and services.
The broader aim has been to strengthen people’s ability to make informed choices and become more independent.
Building Trust, Sharing Learning
For Priti, meaningful social change requires patience. Communities cannot simply be approached with an outside solution and expected to participate immediately. Trust has to be built over time.
Even in the early years, convincing mothers to send their children to Prerana’s Night Care Centres required demonstrating that the organisation was not trying to separate them from their children. It was creating a safe environment where children could be protected while their mothers worked.
Over time, Priti’s work also reinforced her belief that people closest to a problem must be part of its solution. Mothers, children and communities have shaped Prerana’s learning, while collaboration with government agencies, police, schools and other civil-society organisations has helped extend that learning.
She believes social change cannot belong to one organisation alone. Interventions need to be shared, documented and adapted so that successful approaches can reach more people.
Measuring Success Through Choices
For Priti, the success of an intervention cannot be reduced to the number of children reached.
Prerana looks at whether children remain safe, connected to education and supported in their health and psychosocial needs. It also follows individual journeys, including educational progress and barriers that can lead to children dropping out of school.
But there is another measure that matters deeply to her: whether a person’s choices have expanded.
The Night Care Centre, which has benefited thousands of children over the years, represents this philosophy. Some children have gone on to pursue higher education, find employment and build lives different from what society once assumed would be their destiny.
For Priti, that is the larger purpose of child protection. It is not simply about removing a child from a dangerous situation. It is about creating safety, support and opportunities so that the child can imagine and choose a future beyond the circumstances into which they were born.
The Logical Indian Perspective
Priti Patkar’s journey began with witnessing an uncomfortable reality in Kamathipura and asking what could be done differently. Her work with Prerana has since focused on a principle that runs through her approach to child protection: rescue can be only the beginning.
From creating safe spaces at night to supporting education, healthcare, rehabilitation and family relationships, the focus has remained on disrupting intergenerational exploitation without taking away a child’s agency.
Her experience also shows why lasting social change requires more than individual interventions. It demands trust, community participation, institutional collaboration and a willingness to learn from the people closest to the problem.
At the heart of Priti’s work is a simple idea: every child deserves safety, dignity and the freedom to decide what they want their life to become.

title: Jews once lived lived here: When houses tell stories
content:
Jews once lived lived here: When houses tell stories
September 17, 2026Over the years, many people have passed through this fourth-floor apartment in an old Berlin building. Here, at Rosenheimer Straße 40, they have sat on the sofa and gathered around the kitchen table. They have looked out the window and let their minds wander.
Marie Rolshoven has lived here with her family since 2007. "The feeling of crossing that threshold, the same one the former residents crossed for the last time, stays with you," she says. She knows that Jews once lived here, and none of them survived the Nazi era.
Driven from their homes
After the National Socialists seized power in January 1933, it quickly became clear that Jews were considered second-class citizens under Nazi rule. Even the right to remain in their homes could no longer be taken for granted.
"A racially conscious fellow citizen cannot be expected to share a household with a Jew," the Nazi party newspaper Völkischer Beobachter wrote on September 18, 1938, claiming that landlords were therefore entitled to terminate leases without notice. On April 30, 1939, the law took effect. Jewish tenants and property owners were forced to leave their homes and move into buildings designated by the authorities, referred to in Nazi jargon as "Judenhäuser"(Jewish houses).
Several people were forcibly housed in Henny and Carl Möller's apartment at Rosenheimer Straße 40. In the end, there were nine of them. In the fall of 1941, Nazi authorities began systematically deporting Jews to ghettos and camps in Eastern Europe.
Propaganda Minister Joseph Goebbels wrote in his diary: "The main thing is that the capital of the Reich be cleansed of Jews; and I will neither rest nor relent until this goal is fully achieved." The residents of Rosenheimer Straße were among those who were subsequently deported.
Remembering at the original site
Marie Rolshoven aims to honor the fate of these individuals. In 2016, she, along with her late mother and a friend, founded the initiative Denk Mal Am Ort (a wordplay meaning both "Think about it at the site" and "Memorial at the Site") inspired by the Amsterdam project Open Jewish Homes.
The idea is to invite people to the very location where everyday life once occurred. "You feel a strong connection to these individuals through the actual site," says Rolshoven. "It's different from visiting a memorial."
'My brother's bed used to be right here'
Two floors below, her neighbors had a similar experience. Denk Mal Am Ort found out that the Jewish Katzenellenbogen family had previously rented the apartment.
The family escaped Nazi Germany in 1939, just in time. "In 2018, 92-year-old Joel Ludwig Katzenellenbogen was invited back here, accompanied by his daughter, son-in-law, and grandson,” Rolshoven tells DW.
The Denk Mal Am Ort initiative discovered him through Facebook. Rolshoven recounts how touched the visitors were when the former resident walked in and remarked, "Yes, I remember it clearly. My brother's bed used to be right here. He was 10 when we had to leave the country."
Soon there will be no eyewitnesses left
Joel Ludwig Katzenellenbogen has since passed away, along with many other eyewitnesses. This highlights the importance of intergenerational remembrance, according to Rolshoven. She has already welcomed a descendant of a former resident into her home.
Claudia Samter's mother managed to escape from Berlin to Argentina, but her aunt was not as fortunate. Seeking assistance in tracing her family's history, Claudia contacted Denk Mal Am Ort. It turned out that her aunt had once been housed in Rolshoven's apartment.
Claudia Samter has already visited twice. "After all, there's no grave in a cemetery for her to visit," says Rolshoven. "We sat at the kitchen table to talk about life today and tomorrow, and we laughed a lot and cried, too. It felt good to give this space a new purpose once again."
Denk Mal Am Ort has so far organized 90 commemorative events in eight cities this year. Many young descendants attended, according to Rolshoven. "Knowing that they had stood in this stairwell and touched the same doorknob helped them."
Seeking traces of ancestors
19-year-old Adam Ethan Klein from Switzerland also wanted to learn more about his ancestors' history. "I always knew there was a story of escape, but it was never a significant topic at home,” he says.
"They'd say, ‘Yes, your great-grandparents left Germany in 1938, just in time. Luckily, otherwise you wouldn't be here today'."
Klein says his decision to dig deeper was prompted by the spread ofantisemitism, as well as the widespread slogan "Never again is now." (Editor's note: This slogan serves as a call to actively confront antisemitism, hatred, and threats to democracy today.)
The whole family was aware of a suitcase belonging to his maternal great-grandfather in the attic. However, no one ever looked inside until Adam finally opened the suitcase and discovered dozens of documents. He also found a letter from the Hanover District Court dated June 12, 1933, addressed to his great-grandfather, attorney Max Haas.
The letter stated: "As of today, following the decree issued by the Minister of Justice, you have been removed from the list of licensed attorneys."
'They were above all one thing: Jews'
Klein was profoundly affected by the letter: "With this single sentence, it became unmistakably clear to the families that they were not quite what they had aspired to be for generations: an average German family. From that moment on, they were above all one thing: Jews."
For Klein, this was a troubling realization. So was the news that someone had stabbed an ultra-Orthodox Jew to death in Zurich while shouting antisemitic slogans. The attack occurred not far from the synagogue where he had shortly before celebrated a cousin's bar mitzvah. (Editor's note: In Judaism, a bar mitzvah is a ceremony that marks a young person's coming of age in religious matters.)
"For the first time in my life, I felt that unsettling sensation of not quite belonging. Yet Zurich is my home, the city where I've lived carefree as a Jewish Swiss from birth," Adam would later write.
"That was definitely new, uncharted territory for me. I had always thought that such things don't happen in Switzerland. Maybe that was a bit naive of me," he admits.
The subject would not let him go. Adam continued his research, determined to write his high school graduation thesis about his relatives. In the spring of 2024, he set off with his parents, sister, grandmother, uncles, aunts and several cousins to visit the places where their ancestors had lived.
A magical encounter
At some point during their journey, they found themselves in Stuttgart, standing in front of a five-story building at Hölderlinstraße 55, when a man on a bike emerged from the courtyard and approached them.
"So, are you taking a guided tour of the city, or are you planning to move here?" he asked jokingly. The man was Thomas Koch, who had spent time researching the former residents of his house. When he heard the answer, "No, we're just checking out where our ancestors lived," he was thrilled.
Koch had already discovered that the former owners of the house, the Merzbacher brothers, sold it in 1936 for 75,000 Reichsmarks. From that amount, they had to pay 70,000 Reichsmarks in wealth taxes and the Reich Emigration Tax. The remaining sum was just enough to cover the ship fares to Brazil and the United States.
From 1937 to 1938, a family named Hirschheimer, who worked in the plywood trade, lived on the ground floor before they were forcibly relocated to a "Judenhaus." Their trail went cold in 1939, as Koch found no further records. So, he asked, "Are you the Hirschheimer family?" They were indeed.
Koch describes the encounter as magical. Adolf and Auguste Hirschheimer were Adam's great-great-grandparents, and their daughter, Ilse, was married to Max Haas.
Adam Klein and Thomas Koch have kept in touch since then. The next time Adam visited Stuttgart, he was invited over for coffee and cake.
Adam was impressed by the beautiful apartment. "It was fascinating to imagine how my ancestors once lived there, and it probably wasn't that different. Back then, there was likely coffee and cake as well."
Adam showed Koch photos of his grandmother, Ilse, who had married at the synagogue in Stuttgart, standing in the living room in her wedding gown. "In front of the door that we still have," says Koch.
“It was really moving to discover new roommates in a historical context set in the past. And I think this experience — this process of putting myself in their shoes — is a deeply empathetic one that simply brings us together through this apartment.”
Shattered identities
Ilse and Max Haas found refuge in England, while the Hirschheimers emigrated to Switzerland in 1939. Adolf Hirschheimer died in 1940 from a heart condition, but Adam, his great-great-grandson, believes he "certainly also died of a broken heart."
Auguste was brought to England by her son-in-law, Max, where the family felt homesick. "There, we were the Jews; here, we are the Germans. Try figuring that out," Ilse Haas wrote to a friend. Adam chose these lines as the title for his thesis.
Adam's great-grandparents could not find peace after being stripped of their homeland. From England, they eventually went to Israel and, at some point, returned to Europe — to Switzerland.
"At the end of their lives, my great-grandparents settled just a two-hour drive from their old homeland," Adam wrote. "When I look at their lives through the eyes of a great-grandson, it becomes clear that after breaking ties with Germany, they never managed to put down roots anywhere again."
"Remembering is important because, ultimately, we have to learn from history," says Adam. "And I think every single person has a responsibility— and the power — to actively keep memories alive. And hopefully, that can happen even without eyewitnesses.” For example, in his ancestors' former apartment.
This article was originally written in German.

title: De la sabiduría lunar al Whatsapp: la información climática que salvó las cosechas de los agricultores ecuatorianos
content:
- En Ecuador, más de 15 000 agricultores usan los boletines climáticos didácticos para planificar sus siembras y sus cosechas.
- Entre 2022 y 2025, el Instituto Nacional de Meteorología e Hidrología del Ecuador (Inamhi) pasó de emitir 51 advertencias climáticas a 70, confirmando que los cambios en el clima van en aumento.
- La información climática permite prevenir y gestionar el riesgo de desastres y tomar mejores decisiones en agricultura para garantizar la seguridad alimentaria.
- Nuna, un chatbot, ha abierto las opciones de compartir con agricultores de la provincia de Imbabura información climática más allá de las predicciones meteorológicas.
El domingo, Evita Tupiza, la señora que tiene las vacas, la que hace el queso y lo vende el domingo en el mercado de San Blas, en la provincia de Imbabura, le dijo a Gladys Flores que el boletín meteorológico que recibe por WhatsApp la está ayudando a decidir si ordeña o no en las madrugadas. Este no es un asunto trivial para Tupiza: hacerlo bajo el sol fuerte, daña la leche y después no puede producir quesos. Saber con tiempo si va a llover o si habrá altas temperaturas, también le ayuda a prever lugares de sombra para dejar sus vacas en las mañanas.
Hasta hace diez años, quizá cinco, a Evita Tupiza le hubiese bastado con mirar a la luna. En San Blas, una parroquia rural de alrededor de 5000 personas, los agricultores se manejaban a través de “cabañuelas”, cálculos ancestrales en que, observando las variaciones atmosféricas de los primeros días del mes de enero, podían pronosticar el tiempo de los próximos doce meses. Los que sabían leer, acudirían al almanaque Bristol, ese famoso folleto naranja con el doctor Cyrenius Charles Bristol en la portada llevando un traje de hace casi dos siglos. Esta revista que se imprime ininterrumpidamente desde 1832, trae predicciones astronómicas, astrológicas, el calendario lunar y consejos para la siembra
Sin embargo, ahora ni las cabañuelas, ni el almanaque, ni la luna aciertan en sus predicciones del clima, según manifiestan con desconcierto los agricultores de San Blas.
Leer más |Santa Martha: una comunidad cacataibo de Perú cercada por el narcotráfico y el recorte territorial
Como Gaby Flores y Evita Tupiza, alrededor de 15 000 agricultores en Ecuador ―según un informe del Programa Mundial de Alimentos― han mejorado, potenciado o salvado sus cosechas, su tierra y sus animales, gracias a los boletines meteorológicos que líderes comunitarios, servidores públicos de las prefecturas y comuneros capacitados, comparten en los grupos de WhatsApp.
Como una especie de guardianes del clima, estas personas masifican informes que, de manera digerible, explican los datos que el Instituto Nacional de Meteorología e Hidrología del Ecuador (Inamhi) produce en tiempo real. Esto es un asunto vital para los ecuatorianos ya que en los últimos cinco años los eventos climáticos extremos han ido en aumento. Entre 2022 y 2025, el Inamhi pasó de emitir 51 advertencias climáticas a 70.
Información y buenas decisiones
La frontera de Ecuador y Colombia fue el punto de partida de un proyecto ambicioso de adaptación climática incentivado por el Programa Mundial de Alimentos (WFP por sus siglas en inglés) en coordinación con gobiernos locales y otras instituciones públicas. Inició en 2018 con el objetivo de fortalecer las capacidades adaptativas alrededor de las dos cuencas hidrográficas que cruzan y unen los dos países, la Mira-Mataje y la Guáitara-Carchi.
Estas zonas incluyen dos departamentos colombianos y cuatro provincias ecuatorianas con población mayoritariamente indígena y afrodescendiente asentadas en cinco ecosistemas frágiles: manglares, bosques secos, bosques tropicales húmedos, bosques nublados y matorrales; que ya venían sufriendo las variabilidades climáticas del calentamiento global.
Durante seis años se realizaron decenas de colaboraciones estratégicas. Formación a líderes comunitarios, especialmente mujeres, en procesos participativos de 97 comunidades afrodescendientes y 76 comunidades indígenas Awá. Se instalaron 30 equipos meteorológicos, se coordinaron encuentros binacionales, se realizaron rescates de saberes ancestrales, se documentaron más de 350 especies de plantas nativas o tradicionales con atributos nutricionales y nueve boletines climáticos comenzaron a circular entre las 24 000 personas que participaron en las capacitaciones sobre cambio climático. Pasaron una pandemia, el aumento de la violencia en Ecuador, la presencia de grupos armados en la frontera con Colombia y, sin embargo, desde 2024 se comenzaron a ver los frutos que parten de un empoderamiento social de los datos científicos.
“Si tú no tienes información, no vas a poder tomar buenas decisiones, vas a estar corriendo en círculos porque no sabes a qué te estás enfrentando, a qué amenaza y en qué nivel de exposición estás”, dice Diego Guzmán, oficial de cambio climático y sistemas agroalimentarios de WPF. La idea aplica a varios aspectos de la vida, pero Guzmán se refiere a los factores climáticos que perturban, en mayor medida, a comunidades no preparadas para asumir los nuevos escenarios ecológicos.
Esto lo corroboran dos técnicos sentados en una oficina austera de muros cremas del segundo piso del edificio de la prefectura de Imbabura.
Edison Marcial y Vinicio Fuentes asistieron a varias de las capacitaciones de sistemas de manejo de datos meteorológicos que dictaron especialistas del Inamhi. Les explicaron lo más complicado y teórico de los procesos científicos de la meteorología: qué satélites se usan, cómo hacen las agencias nacionales los pronósticos del tiempo, qué son los modelos matemáticos de predicción, las plataformas digitales en las que se procesan los datos, los mapas de color y el monitoreo en tiempo real en el Visor Hidrometeorológico Nacional.
“Es de acceso público toda la información”, dice Edison Marcial, mientras muestra una imagen en su teléfono celular: un mapa de la provincia de Imbabura con unos aros de colores, en la gama del verde al rojo. “El Inamhi te manda así, la imagen en bruto”.
El WPF hizo que personal del propio Inamhi capacitara a dos funcionarios de cada provincia en Ecuador y departamento en Colombia. El objetivo era que los técnicos locales entendieran los modelos de predicción oficiales y los tradujeran de tal manera que cualquier persona los pudiera interpretar. Fue así que la primera parte del proyecto de creación de boletines climáticos, en 2024, dio como resultado nueve boletines (entre semanales y diarios) que llegaron a compartirse entre 15 000 agricultores de los dos países.
Los primeros boletines salvaron las cosechas
En 2024, Ecuador rompió los récord de temperaturas altas con sequías extremas: más de 80 000 hectáreas quemadas y una grave crisis energética, según datos de la Secretaría Nacional de Riesgos. Ese mismo año, los boletines meteorológicos didácticos comenzaron a circular cada tres días, en las provincias de Carchi, Imbabura, Esmeraldas y Sucumbíos. Se trataba de una imagen con el mapa de la provincia y la intensidad de las lluvias. Una leyenda de seis colores que variaba desde el rojo (que significa lluvias intensas) y el verde en el medio (señal de lluvia moderada), hasta llegar al blanco que indica ausencia total de lluvia. A un costado se mostraban las temperaturas máximas y mínimas.
Esto evitó pérdidas en la zona del Valle del Chota y en la zona de Urcuquí, en la Provincia de Imbabura, donde está el terreno familiar de Gladys Flores, hija, nieta y bisnieta de campesinos.
“Cuando era pequeña, mi bisabuela me contaba que sus padres también fueron agricultores en este mismo terreno”, dice Flores mientras recorre sus sembríos, mostrándolos con orgullo. Es la quinta generación que trabaja esa tierra.
En su casa de ladrillos, madera y techo de Eternit, ella y su esposo, César Vinueza, comparten una limonada y sus experiencias en el campo. Cuentan que el agua que riega sus productos es muy limpia porque viene cinco kilómetros arriba del río Warmiyaku, dónde está la captación.
“Esa piscina de captación y la acequia [canal artificial a cielo abierto] es de antes de la venida de los españoles. Es muy antigua”, comenta Flores.“Mi papá sabía con exactitud cuándo venía el verano y la época seca. Ahora llueve cuando no es de llover. Encima, el caudal del río ha bajado bastante. Antes no podíamos controlar la fuerza del agua cuando nos tocaba el turno del riego. Ahora baja poquito. Toca estar yendo a ver qué pasa en la captación y que todo esté bien”.
Leer más | Día Internacional de los Primates: tres proyectos para salvarlos del tráfico y la pérdida de hábitat
Con menos agua de riego y más sequía, Flores, su esposo y todo el pueblo de San Blas están “cosechando agua”, es decir, llenan unos tanques enormes de plástico que recuperan el agua cuando llueve.
“En 2024 vino fuerte la sequía. Nos tocó hacer turnos con las demás compañeras. Cada 15 días recibimos el agua de la acequia para regar nuestros terrenos. Justo en ese tiempo llegaron los boletines y, viendo en las fotos que iba a estar seca la época que normalmente era de lluvia, atrasamos el cultivo del fréjol. Gracias a esas cartillas no perdimos tanto de nuestro trabajo”, recuerda Gladys Flores.
César Vinueza, el esposo de Gladys, cuenta que la casa en la que viven fue construida para un lugar frío, cerca a los páramos que es donde se asienta San Blas. Sin embargo, el calor actual es tan fuerte que el techo que tenía que guardar el calor, ahora lo acumula de tal manera que tienen que hacer ciertos cambios. “Estoy preocupado, nunca me imaginé que el Eternit fuera tan caliente. A la una de la tarde es insoportable, por eso voy a arreglar esas dos ventanas para que entre el aire directo, como casa de la costa”.
Todos ríen.
Flores y Vinueza se juntaron con otras mujeres agricultoras para crear la asociación agropecuaria “Frutos de mi Tierra”. Casi llegan a los 10 años llevando sus productos a la feria del pueblo los domingos y los miércoles en la Universidad Yachay.
Leer más | Eric Terena, el DJ indígena que denuncia el silenciamiento de la Amazonía | ENTREVISTA
“Nuestro principal orgullo es que hemos eliminado a los intermediarios, de aquí salen los productos directo a los compradores”, dice Vinueza.
Gladys Flores administra el grupo de WhatsApp de la asociación y es la encargada de compartir, cada tres días, el boletín climático que la prefectura de Imbabura le envía a ella.
Desde que se dieron cuenta que con esa información pudieron evitar una siembra de fréjol que se perdería por la sequía inesperada de 2024, las mujeres de Frutos de mi Tierra son acérrimas usuarias del boletín que, en dos años, tuvo una cadena de innovaciones que superó las expectativas de los propios organismos estatales y de cooperación internacional que iniciaron el proyecto en 2018.
Flores cuenta que gracias a los videos que reciben con los pronósticos y las alertas climáticas, las mujeres campesinas que no saben leer y escribir ya no tienen que mostrar la infografía colorida a sus hijos o nietos para que confirmen lo que ellas ven en colores, sino que con el audio ya “entienden todito”. Y que esa información, como le dijo Evita Tupiza, le ha permitido planificar el ordeño de sus vacas para la producción de los quesos.
El aficionado al arte que prepara a los agricultores
Vinicio Fuentes es agrónomo y tiene un máster en sistemas de información geográfica, pero habla como productor de televisión o creador de contenidos.
Sentado frente a su computadora, busca emocionado los primeros videos que creó a partir de los pronósticos oficiales del Inamhi. Fuentes no se conformó con mandar el boletín de colores y fue más allá. Primero, le puso voz y animó la imagen. De inmediato se dio cuenta que los agricultores comenzaron a estar pendientes de la información.
“Lo que siempre estoy pensando es: ¿cómo hago digeribles todos estos datos? Por suerte han tenido la paciencia de permitirme la prueba y el error”, cuenta Fuentes con una sonrisa disimulada que muestra cómo disfruta de su trabajo.
Uno de los problemas más frecuentes que enfrentó en sus procesos de comunicación era que la persona que hacía las locuciones no estaba siempre disponible para cuando el boletín climático comenzó a ser un ritual. Entonces Fuentes probó con una voz de inteligencia artificial. Esto fue un éxito porque le permitió hacer más eficiente la producción de los boletines cada tres días. Con el tiempo, y con las pruebas, también se dio cuenta que los videos debían ser más cortos para que no fueran “tan pesados” y los usuarios pudieran abrirlos desde sus teléfonos.
“Lo que la gente necesita saber es si va a llover o no”, dice con la seguridad de la experiencia, Edison Marcial, quien fue parte del Programa Mundial de Alimentos antes de trabajar en la prefectura de Imbabura. Asegura ser testigo de cómo el interés de Vinicio Fuentes y sus ganas de mejorar los boletines hicieron que Imbabura fuera pionera de iniciativas mucho más ambiciosas como “Nuna”, el chatbot, o la Granja Digital, una plataforma con datos públicos y accesibles con los cuales los productores de Imbabura pueden consultar información sobre sus predios, la fertilidad de sus suelos y buenas prácticas agrícolas.
“Vimos que WhatsApp es uno de los medios masivos de comunicación entre las comunidades agrícolas”, comenta Fuentes mientras conecta su computadora a una pantalla gigante en la oficina de uno de sus jefes para mostrar cómo funciona el chatbot que creó.
Con un grupo de creativos dieron vida a un personaje que suma todas las características culturales de los diferentes pueblos de Imbabura. Se llama Nuna y significa “alma” o “energía vital” en kichwa. Tiene la máscara tradicional de diablo huma pero con plumas de los colibríes que existen en los diferentes cantones de la provincia.
“La idea fue tener un chat en el que puedes hacer consultas continuamente y ya no ser un usuario pasivo que recibe los boletines”, dice Fuentes con orgullo.
En la pantalla se abre la conversación. ¡Hola, soy Nuna, tu asistente virtual de la Prefectura de Imbabura, gracias por tu mensaje! Nuna abre una serie de opciones: Geoparque Imbabura, Clima, Ferias Productoras, Rutas Turísticas, Novedades, Smartfarm y Servicios Mecánicos.
“Aprovechamos que tenemos toda esta lógica de comunicación a partir del boletín climático, que fue el inicio de esto, para potenciar y difundir toda la información que tenemos como Prefectura”, explica Fuentes.
Al dar click a la opción “Clima”, Nuna comparte el video del boletín agroclimático de Imbabura, las advertencias meteorológicas nacionales del Inamhi (información adicional sobre eventos intensos de lluvias o sequías) y el calendario lunar, como una forma de incluir y respetar la diversidad cultural.
Desde el 1 de enero al 31 de mayo de 2026, el Inamhi había registrado 2026 eventos adversos como inundaciones, deslizamientos y aluviones.
Leer más | Antártida: cierran la pesquería de kril por sobrepesca y crece la alerta por sus impactos
El aprendizaje se aprovecha y se comparte en cadena
Esta nueva forma de entregar información climática está llegando a todo el país. El 4 de junio de 2026, PWF, Inamhi, Ministerio de Ambiente y Energía y representantes de las prefecturas de Imbabura y Manabí ―provincia ecuatoriana costera que sufre inundaciones continuas― se reunieron en la Capilla del Hombre, en Quito. Era el lanzamiento oficial de los boletines nacionales del Inamhi. “De la información climática a la acción territorial” se llamó el evento
Vinicio Fuentes, muy tímido, parado al fondo de la sala con los brazos echados para atrás, escuchaba las intervenciones de las autoridades, de los científicos y el testimonio de Juan De Mera Centeno, agricultor de la asociación Raíces Manabas que produce principalmente arroz, verduras, hortalizas y frutas en Manabí. “Al tener acceso a esta información optimizamos tiempo y recursos. Por ejemplo, para el trasplante de una semilla, si sabemos que va a llover, ponemos en pausa el trabajo porque inundado el suelo, todo se pierde”, dice el campesino de la costa ecuatoriana.
Manabí es la segunda provincia que hace los boletines meteorológicos con video para alrededor de 9000 agricultores.
“No fue fácil motivar a la prefectura de Manabí para que haga los boletines metereológicos”, confiesa Diego Guzmán de PWF. “Allá no creen, o no creían―Guzmán suelta una risa― en la cooperación internacional”.
Fue entonces cuando invitaron a Vinicio Fuentes a la Prefectura de la provincia costera. Él contó su experiencia a Jairo Moreira, su par, el encargado de compartir la información que recibe del Inamhi a las diferentes organizaciones de agricultores de Manabí.
“El PWF nos dio el equipamiento, un ordenador con un programa de edición de video. El Inamhi nos capacitó para interpretar los datos y los mapas que nos envían. El ingeniero Vinicio nos enseñó cómo ellos hacen los videos con palabras más sencillas. Así iniciamos la producción de los boletines aquí”, confirma Moreira.
Y pasó algo que no esperaba: los usuarios de Manabí tampoco se pierden un solo boletín. Al igual que en Imbabura, el video corto y didáctico ha hecho que sus agricultores usen esta información como parte de su trabajo. A partir de los boletines toman decisiones sobre sus tierras y sus productos.
Por ejemplo, si ven que va a llover, los productores de cacao no sacan a secar sus semillas. También les ayuda a planificar la época de siembra y de cosecha de productos de ciclo corto.
“Esto lo implementamos en diciembre de 2024 y el testimonio de los agricultores es que, con esta información hacen mucho mejor su trabajo porque pueden adaptarse a las variaciones climáticas”, dice Moreira y agrega que cuando se demoran y no envían el boletín a tiempo, los campesinos usuarios los llaman, los presionan y les preguntan qué pasó con el boletín. “Ha tenido muy buena aceptación. Ahora nos lo piden asociaciones que están fuera de los grupos de la Prefectura. También estudiantes de universidades y otras federaciones de campesinos”.
Ese 4 de junio en La Capilla del Hombre, uno de los complejos arquitectónicos y culturales más importantes de Quito, Matteo Perrone, representante de PWF para Ecuador, dijo a una sala llena que uno de los principales logros del proyecto de adaptación al cambio climático en Ecuador fue la descentralización del conocimiento.
Luego, pasaron un video hecho por los técnicos del Inhami. Tomando la idea de la prefectura de Imbabura, ahora los boletines nacionales también se harán en video con una voz en IA que cuenta lo que significan los colores en el mapa de calor.
Pocos entre la gente del evento saben que el hombre que está de pie al otro lado del escenario, con las manos echadas para atrás, que le gusta tocar guitarra, piano y editar los boletines climáticos en CapCut, es Vinicio Fuentes, quien, con su motivación, logró que se replique la forma de informar y dar herramientas a los agricultores que él inició hace algún tiempo desde Imbabura.

title: In Paash’s village, a fight over the space that keeps his memory alive
content:

The words of Avtar Singh Sandhu, better known as Paash, have travelled far beyond Talwandi Salem, his birthplace in Jalandhar district. Nearly four decades after he was killed, his poetry continues to surface wherever people gather around democratic rights and resistance — at farmers’ protests, workers’ meetings, student gatherings and literary forums.
For generations of readers, Paash was not merely a poet who wrote about struggle; he was a poet who participated in it.
Ahead of his birth anniversary on September 9, however, his legacy has become the centre of a dispute in his native village. Tension erupted after the village panchayat allegedly tried to stop members of the Paash-Hans Raj Memorial Committee from erecting a pandal at an eponymous complex for the celebrations. Allegations of manhandling prompted the local administration to deploy police to prevent a confrontation.
The dispute centres around two kanals of land at the entrance of Talwandi Salem, where the Pash-Hans Raj Memorial has stood for 26 years. The committee says the land was allotted to it in 2000 through a written panchayat resolution. The panchayat, however, maintains that the land belongs to it.
The confrontation dates back to early August, when the Paash Memorial International Trust, the Paash-Hans Raj Shaheedi Yaadgar Committee and several unions approached the Nakodar SDM and local MLA with allegations of vandalism. According to their complaint, panchayat representatives broke the locks of the memorial gate. When the committee replaced them, one side of the gate was allegedly removed and panchayat representatives entered the premises and installed swings, pipes and open-gym equipment.
Local administrative officials initially maintained that the land belonged to the panchayat, while indicating that the matter was close to resolution. The dispute flared again when committee members arrived to prepare for Paash’s September 9 birth anniversary. A group led by sarpanch Pardeep Singh allegedly confronted them, including veteran activist Jhanda Singh Jethuke. Committee members alleged that some activists were pushed and that mobile phones were confiscated.
For villagers and Paash’s admirers, the confrontation has taken on a larger meaning. “It is a great disrespect to a great poet, and that too by the people and the panchayat of his own village,” said a local resident.
The memorial complex was initially undeveloped land. According to trust members, it was transformed over the years through voluntary contributions from admirers in Punjab and abroad, including supporters in the US, Canada and the UK. Today, the site includes an open-air theatre, green rooms and a library housing Paash’s writings, besides basic utilities. It has hosted memorial programmes, theatre performances and literary gatherings.
Paash and his close friend Hans Raj were assassinated by militants on March 23, 1988. Paash was 37. The committee says it has no objection to recreational facilities for villagers but argues that a cultural institution built over decades should not be altered without consultation.
“The issue is not about opposing swings or an open gym,” said Amolak Singh, trustee and committee member. “The question is why these facilities must be installed inside a memorial when the village has other public parks. There is no reason to disturb its character.”
He also questioned the circumstances in which the locks and part of the gate were allegedly removed and recreational equipment installed in the complex.
This year’s birth anniversary celebrations are planned both at the memorial and at the site where Paash and Hans Raj were killed, in the fields near a tubewell in the village.
Born on September 9, 1950, Paash emerged as one of modern Punjabi literature’s most distinctive voices. His poetry placed workers, farmers and the disenfranchised at the centre of literary expression. Sab Ton Khatarnak (The Most Dangerous), his best-known poem, remains a powerful warning against apathy and the loss of conscience.
Dr Kuldeep Singh, a Punjabi literature scholar and former professor at Punjabi University, Patiala, said Paash’s enduring influence could be compared with that of Faiz Ahmed Faiz and Pablo Neruda.
“Paash belongs to the people. Whenever resistance emerges, his poetry returns. His legacy should be expanded through a meaningful memorial, not reduced to a petty land dispute,” he said.
“His poems questioned oppression, communalism and the silencing of dissent, and his own life reflected that spirit of resistance. During the turbulent years of militancy in Punjab, he openly opposed Khalistani extremism and used his writing to challenge communal politics’,” he added.
His family is now working to preserve another part of that history. His wife and daughter, based in the US, have dedicated two acres of ancestral land — including the site near the tubewell where Paash and Hans Raj were killed — to the Avtar Singh Paash Memorial Trust for a second memorial.
For Sucha Singh, convenor of the committee and Paash’s cousin, the issue is also one of village identity. “People across the world know Talwandi Salem because Paash was born here,” he said.
The dispute has also raised a broader question about who should protect literary heritage.
Amolak Singh said political figures are often commemorated through government-backed memorials, while the preservation of literary legacies is frequently left to writers, admirers and civil society groups. Farmer, student and labour unions have since launched awareness campaigns in villages to build support for the memorial.
Nakodar SDM Simranjeet Singh said the administration was aware of the confrontation and that police had been deployed to maintain peace during the September 9 programme.
AAP chief spokesperson Neel Garg said the local administration should provide greater clarity on the dispute, while acknowledging that the controversy should not have arisen.
“What is happening in Talwandi Salem should not happen. Paash is an international poet whose work instills the spirit to fight for rights,” Garg said. He added that the matter would be brought to the notice of Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann.

title: Low-cost phone lessons keep children learning during emergency school closures across five countries
content:
The COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns forced people to find ways to get things done remotely. Companies developed systems that made working from home run smoothly. Educators also had to shift to mobile phones and group video calls to get their lessons across and make sure students didn't lose out on their progress. This exposed the need for education systems to be more resilient and adaptive to local and global disruptions.
A recent Nature study explored how low-tech mobile phone programs could keep children learning when schools close because of major emergencies such as disease outbreaks, extreme weather or natural disasters.
Across India, Kenya, Nepal, the Philippines and Uganda, researchers conducted large-scale randomized trials to test remote-learning methods delivered through simple mobile phones.
Adding a weekly, one-on-one, 20-minute phone-call tutorial to text messages led to significant gains in basic math skills across all five countries. Students learned roughly three times more when they received phone calls tailored to their learning level.
The combined phone-call and SMS tutorial program cost just $11 per child. For every $100 spent, it generated 3.6 years of high-quality schooling, putting it among the top 10 most cost-effective education interventions ever evaluated, out of 150 studies worldwide.
Learning must go on
Nearly 25% of the world's population lives in countries where education is at risk of disruption because of political, medical or climate emergencies. A recent report estimated that around 222 million children face regular disruptions to their education, losing precious opportunities to learn and worsening the existing global learning crisis, in which fewer than half of primary-school-age children in low- and middle-income countries can read a simple story or do basic arithmetic.
When schools shut down, education systems need fast, low-cost and flexible ways to keep kids learning. However, rigorous evidence on what actually works during emergencies is rare.
Mobile phones have permeated into most nooks and crannies of the world where humans reside, leading researchers to explore them as a tool for reaching primary school children during emergencies. Wherever there are mobile phones, people can connect via text messages and phone calls, which might feel less efficient than the internet, but more than 70% of households in low-income countries have the former and only 15% have the latter.
Hello, it's math
To find out whether a single mobile-phone-based emergency education strategy could work in different parts of the world, researchers needed a coordinated, multicountry trial. Between December 2020 and July 2022, more than 16,000 households with primary school students from the five countries participated in the remote-learning experiment. Researchers randomly assigned students to different groups to compare levels of remote support.
Students in the control group received no remote tutoring during the trial period. Families in the SMS-only group received weekly text messages containing basic math problems and practice reminders. This group was not tested in India. Students in the phone call and SMS group received the weekly text messages plus a 20-minute, one-on-one phone tutoring session each week for 8–12 weeks.
The phone calls were built around targeted teaching. Each week, instructors used a short assessment during the call to determine what the child could do, then designed the math lesson around those specific needs instead of simply following the grade-level curriculum. At the end of the trial, researchers tested progress using the standard Annual Status of Education Report tool.
Economic yet effective
They found that weekly live tutoring calls paired with text messages delivered large learning gains in basic math across all five countries. On average, students in the phone tutoring program gained 0.321 standard deviations in learning, meaning their gains were three times larger than those of the median education intervention evaluated globally.
The combined phone-call and SMS program led to a 92% jump in the number of students who could correctly solve division problems. Students also improved on more advanced skills, including fractions, where performance increased by 6.4 percentage points.
Uganda and the Philippines saw the biggest improvements, where long school closures left children with few opportunities to continue learning. In Uganda, phone tutoring helped fourth graders make up all the learning they had lost during the pandemic and even outperform fifth graders who did not receive the program.
The researchers found that the approach worked just as well when delivered by government teachers as by nongovernmental organizations, giving them confidence that it can be scaled through public education systems.
The results show that by deploying a low-cost mobile-based intervention strategy, education systems can maintain learning amid disruptions across diverse settings. The approach is now moving into classrooms across Karnataka, India, supporting learning during the school year and keeping children connected when monsoon closures shut schools.

title: ‘A single wrong step’: Women deminers reach where men cannot to protect children in Syria
content:
In a dry field in Syria’s Idlib countryside, Lama Haj Kaddour holds a detonator, steady and practised.
She and her all-female team have spent hours locating and safely approaching a buried landmine. A short distance away, the rest of the team waits, still and silent.
When the blast goes off, a column of smoke rises from where the mine had been.
Kaddour wears a protective vest over her clothes. Like her colleagues, she dresses fully in black with only her eyes visible, in line with social norms in Idlib.
Fourteen years of civil war have left Syria littered with landmines and explosive remnants of war (ERW). The threat has followed families back to the villages they fled, even after the end of a conflict that killed hundreds of thousands, displaced millions and devastated the economy.
Kaddour is one of 31 women now working in operational roles in Idlib’s demining effort, according to The HALO Trust, an international NGO involved in Syria’s demining work.
They clear landmines, survey contaminated ground and teach communities how to recognise the dangers left behind by the civil war.
Kaddour, a 33-year-old mother of three, left the Hama countryside for Idlib in 2019. She first worked with relief organisations before joining The HALO Trust.
In a conservative region like Idlib, being a woman can carry a particular advantage in demining work.
“A woman working in this field can enter local households and speak directly with women and children in ways her male colleagues often cannot, giving her direct access to a part of the community that is otherwise hard to reach in a conservative context,” Emma Pomfret, Global Media Manager for The HALO Trust, tells TRT World.
Women remain a minority in demining worldwide.
A 2019 survey of a dozen mine action operators published by the Journal of Conventional Weapons Destruction found that women made up only around 20 percent of mine action staff globally, with clearance roles particularly male-dominated.
According to Pomfret, however, more women are entering the field in Syria.
The fall of the Assad regime in late 2024 removed severe operational restrictions that had constrained HALO’s work, she says, allowing the organisation to expand training and clearance into areas including Daraa and the northwest and recruit from a much larger pool of people.
“When the Assad regime fell in December 2024, HALO opened recruitment and training to women, as we do on all of our programmes globally,” she says.
Supporting landmine survivors
In training hubs such as Daraa, women now make up about 20 percent of new demining trainees — eight out of a recent class of 40, according to Pomfret. As HALO expands beyond 250 staff nationwide, women are increasingly working as manual deminers, team supervisors, paramedics and community educators.
The shift is not only about new opportunities. Some of the women joining HALO were widowed during the war and are now the main breadwinners for their families, Pomfret says.
Kaddour's own path into demining began earlier. She started by supporting landmine survivors before training for fieldwork in 2022 and taking on the work of clearing unexploded ordnance herself.
“I could never live with the idea that a single wrong step by my children could set off a landmine that ends their lives, or takes one of their limbs,” Kaddour tells TRT World.
More than three million displaced people have returned to areas badly damaged by the conflict. Many find their homes still standing, but the roads leading to them contaminated.
Raed al-Hassoun, director of clearance operations at Syria’s National Mine Action Centre, tells TRT World that 49 landmine incidents were recorded across the country between the start of 2026 and the end of August, killing 24 people and injuring 61.
On August 31, an unexploded object detonated in the village of Faydat Ibn Muwaina in the Deir Ezzor countryside as children were handling it. Four children were killed and one was injured, according to SANA.
The Syrian Network for Human Rights (SNHR) says at least 3,799 civilians — including 1,000 children and 377 women — have been killed by landmines and cluster munition remnants across Syria since March 2011, with 329 of those deaths recorded since December 2024.
The highest tolls were recorded in Aleppo, with 814 deaths, followed by Raqqa with 676 and Deir Ezzor with 645. Hama, Daraa and Idlib were also among the worst affected.
According to SNHR, the Assad regime, Russian forces and terror groups have planted landmines across Syrian territory since 2011, often without marking or recording their locations.
Siba Abdul Karim, a 36-year-old mother of two who heads the non-technical survey department at The HALO Trust, says floods and heavy rains can expose or move buried mines and other war remnants.
“The danger isn’t necessarily fixed where the war left it,” she tells TRT World
“Floodwater, like what we saw in late August, can reshape the land and carry buried explosive objects with it, rendering old maps insufficient. Ground that seemed safe yesterday can become a fresh hazard after a flood or landslide.”
Abdul Karim and her colleagues have chosen to confront that danger directly.
The women say years of war have made them less afraid of the risks involved in their work.
“Every morning, I say goodbye to my children before leaving for the field. Every evening, when I walk back through the door, I give thanks that I made it home unharmed,” Abdul Karim tells TRT World.
She recalls once calming a child who had found an explosive device, reassuring him before explaining the danger of what he had found.
Also working in the field is Mariam al Asaad, 26, who is married and has an eight-year-old daughter.
For nearly four years, al Asaad has volunteered with the Syrian Civil Defence, also known as the White Helmets, conducting non-technical surveys and risk education and helping map contaminated areas. In 2022, she received specialised training in survey and munitions classification, becoming one of the first women to join Syria’s ERW teams.
Every morning, al Asaad kisses her daughter goodbye before leaving for the field. When she returns home, she faces the challenge of balancing a dangerous job with motherhood.
“I worry all the time about the balance between my daughter and this job,” she tells TRT World.
For al Asaad, the work is also personal. Her father owned land east of Idlib that was contaminated with landmines the family did not know were there.
In 2017, as fighting around Idlib eased, he returned to tend to the family’s olive grove, taking al Asaad’s younger brother, then nine years old, with him.
“A landmine exploded when my brother threw a stone at the ground. It tore into his left foot,” she says.
With no way of knowing how many more mines lay buried there, the family abandoned the land.
“My father spent his final years watching the trees go wild, and the little fruit that still fell just rotted on the ground,” she says. “We ended up buying olive oil every season, even though we had a grove that used to give us our own.”
Al Asaad believes the grief of losing access to the land took a heavy toll on her father’s health.
Waiting for the land back
In the village of Dadikh in the Idlib countryside, Abu Mohammad al Ali, 62, owns land that was once his family’s sole source of livelihood. The war has turned it into a place he can no longer enter.
He grew olive and fruit trees there, relying on the harvest to support his family, before mines and other war remnants contaminated the land.
“We used to come here at first light, plough, plant, and tend to the trees,” al Ali tells TRT World.
“Today I’m afraid to take a single step onto my own land. The trees we worked so hard to grow have died because we can no longer reach them to water them and care for them.”
According to al Ali, his land was the scene of clashes and aerial bombardment during the war.
Assad regime forces, backed by Russian air support, attempted to advance towards the edges of the village but were unable to take the area from local forces.
His land lay along the front line.
Months of fighting left the land heavily contaminated with mines and other remnants of war, making it inaccessible even after the fighting stopped.
“Fear is part of daily life for my family and everyone in the village,” he says.
He recalls an incident in 2025 when a mine exploded on his land while a child was nearby.
Since then, he has struggled with the thought that land that once fed his family could instead kill a child.
“Farmers in Dadikh live between leaving their land and losing their livelihood, or returning to it with the possibility that the next step could be their last,” he says.
“The hardest part is that when I look at my land, I still see it as it used to be. I see the trees, and I remember the seasons we used to wait for. But today I can't get close to it.”
“We just want the mines removed, and to know the land is safe before we send our children there or go back to farming it ourselves,” he adds.
Alongside clearance efforts, UNICEF and its partners are teaching children and families to recognise mine risks before demining teams can reach contaminated areas.
Fouad Mansour, a project manager at UNICEF, tells TRT World that the agency and its partners reached roughly 850,000 children, parents and caregivers with mine-risk education in 2025 and trained around 400 specialists.
“We use pictures, stories, games and visual material to turn a frightening fact into a behaviour a child can remember: don’t touch the strange object, move away from it, and tell an adult or the relevant authority,” he says.
Mansour says UNICEF works with 38 partners across mine clearance, victim assistance, risk education and advocacy.
It has also supported the development of a national risk-education framework integrated into the curriculum in coordination with Syria’s Ministry of Education.
A national effort to bring order
At the national level, Syria’s National Mine Action Centre is coordinating efforts by international and local organisations.
“We are currently developing the national standards that will govern the work of organisations in this field,” Raed al Hassoun says.
“We are also building a national information management system to collect the data that will underpin a roadmap for addressing landmine and ERW risk according to national priorities.”
Among the centre’s priorities is completing a national non-technical survey to determine the location, type and scale of contamination, amid what al Hassoun describes as limited capacity to address the problem's scale.
“Our own figures are still incomplete,” he says, adding that the national survey under way is intended to close that gap.
Military engineering teams from the Ministry of Defence and dedicated units from the Ministry of Emergency and Disaster Management also take part in clearance operations, he says.
“The reconstruction of Syria’s battered infrastructure depends first and foremost on resolving the mine issue,” al Hassoun says, pointing to the Jobar district of Damascus as an example.
At the request of the Damascus governorate, the centre established an operations room that brought together the HALO Trust, the International Committee of the Red Cross, teams from the Ministry of Emergency and Disaster Management, and Red Crescent non-technical survey teams.
Together, they cleared Jobar’s main and side roads, allowing reconstruction work to begin.

title: Tourists put these sea turtle nests at risk. Local Mexicans intervened, and now 3,200 hatchlings are swimming free
content:
On August 30, a Mexican nonprofit dedicated to sea turtle conservation released between 3,200 and 3,500 sea turtles into the Gulf of Mexico from a beach in northern Veracruz.
The nonprofit, Tortugas Fundación Yepez A.C., was founded in 1967 by fisherman Don Marcelino Yepez and his wife Librada Gerón, affectionately known as “Mama Turtle.”
Their legacy lives on as their eldest son, Ricardo Yépez, continues their mission today.
“It’s already August 30, 2026, and well, the moment has arrived — the time has come to see the culmination of sleepless nights, hard work, patrols, [and] all-nighters,” Yépez said in an Instagram Reel.
According to Yépez, tourists were putting nesting sea turtles and their eggs at risk by approaching, touching, and even climbing turtles.
Patrols intensified in August after a pregnant green sea turtle was reported dead on a beach in Nautla, Veracruz. Afterwards, Yépez issued a public warning to tourists to give nesting sea turtles their space, according to reports by La Jornada.
In the weeks since, Yépez and his team of patrollers set up protected sites and moved nests from high-risk areas to small enclosures where they could hatch in peace.
“Today they are being released back into the ocean without any form of harm,” Yépez said, as he crouched on the beach, shoulder to shoulder with his volunteer team. “There aren’t enough words to express our gratitude to all the people who call us, who alert us, and who take responsibility for beach areas.”
“A huge thank you to all these angels whom God has placed in our path so that we can achieve our conservation goals for this endangered little animal,” he continued. “We’re celebrating 59 years of work — it’s easy to say, but it’s 59 years of continuous seasons, of persistence — and thanks be to God, and thanks to all of you, it’s possible for us to continue today. From my parents’ time until today — that’s 59 years now.”
At the end of his speech, Yépez said that there weren’t “enough words” to thank everyone who made the release possible.
“Well, today we’re going to release roughly 3,200 to 3,500 baby turtles,” he said. “Ready, guys? Uno, dos, vámonos!”
In unison, the Tortugas Fundación Yepez A.C. team released the sea turtles onto the sand from their respective buckets. As they raced to the water, the sea turtles tumbled on top of each other and wiggled their flippers, eager to reach the surf.
“Congratulations on your 59 years!” one Instagram user commented. “You say ‘it’s easy,’ but it's a lifetime of dedication and effort that not everyone does.”
