title: Appraising Uba Sani’s Bold Rescue of Kaduna’s Out-of-School Children
content:
Latest Headlines
Appraising Uba Sani’s Bold Rescue of Kaduna’s Out-of-School Children
Abdulkareem Kubau
The truest measure of an education policy is not the elegance of its declarations, but the number of children whose lives it changes. In Kaduna State, Governor Uba Sani has steadily moved education reform from aspiration to measurable action, confronting one of the gravest threats to the state’s future: the exclusion of children from school. His administration has treated the out-of-school crisis neither as an inherited misfortune nor as an insoluble feature of northern Nigeria, but as an emergency demanding money, evidence, competent management and sustained political will.
That seriousness is visible first in the state’s priorities. For three consecutive years, education has received the largest single share of Kaduna’s budget. The sector took 25 per cent in 2024, 26.14 per cent in 2025 and 25 per cent of the N985.9 billion 2026 budget. In a public culture where education is frequently celebrated in speeches but weakened in expenditure, this consistency matters. It has given institutional weight to the administration’s conviction that Kaduna cannot defeat poverty, insecurity, unemployment or social exclusion without first enlarging access to knowledge.
The investment supports a broader architecture of reform. Tuition fees in state-owned tertiary institutions were halved, contributing to an enrolment rise exceeding 200 per cent. The retirement age for teachers moved from 60 to 65, while the state committed to recruiting 2,000 primary school teachers annually. Across the 23 local government areas, thousands of classrooms have been built or renovated and essential facilities, furniture and learning materials provided. School feeding has strengthened retention, while extensive education data capture has improved planning.
Yet the defining strength of the Governor Sani approach is its recognition that improved schools alone cannot solve exclusion. A classroom may exist while the poorest child remains unable to enter it. Tuition may be free while uniforms, books, transport, levies and the loss of a child’s labour place education beyond a family’s means.
In Kaduna’s household mapping, economic constraints accounted for 58.5 per cent of exclusion, and lack of money dominated the reasons given within that category. “Free education” therefore describes a legal entitlement; it does not erase the real price borne by vulnerable households.
This understanding places the Reaching Out-of-School Children Project at the heart of the Governor Sani administration’s education agenda. ROOSC is not a ceremonial programme or isolated donor initiative. It expresses Governor Sani’s determination to find excluded children, understand why each is outside the classroom, remove the barrier and create a pathway into sustained learning. Valued at $62.8 million and operating across all 23 local government areas, the four-year intervention combines state funding with grants and technical support.
Its ambition is substantial. ROOSC aims to enrol 100,000 out-of-school children and benefit 1.2 million learners. It provides for 102 new schools and learning centres, 170 renovations and work on 2,304 classrooms. It will strengthen school-based management committees, train teachers and officers, improve learning outcomes and make schools safer and more inclusive. Civil works have commenced, but the project’s reach extends beyond buildings.
Children who cannot immediately return through conventional schooling are offered flexible routes. Accelerated basic education enables older learners to recover lost years. Integrated Qur’anic and Tsangaya education combines religious instruction with literacy, numeracy and life skills. Catch-up clubs prepare dropouts for re-entry, while radio lessons reach difficult terrain. Vulnerable learners receive materials, girls receive menstrual-health support, and children with disabilities receive assessment and assistive devices. This is reform shaped around the child, not a demand that every child fit one rigid system.
Early results justify the confidence now surrounding ROOSC. More than 26,000 out-of-school children have been enrolled cumulatively, with boys and girls represented in near-equal numbers. Thousands more have been reached through accelerated education, integrated learning, catch-up clubs and radio instruction. Over 1,600 catch-up learners have moved into formal schools, while the first accelerated-learning cohort recorded retention of nearly 85 per cent. Teachers, head teachers and quality-assurance officers have received structured professional development, with recorded competency gains. These are not abstract outputs; they are children restored to possibility and schools acquiring the capacity to keep them there.
The project’s most consequential achievement may be its replacement of estimates with evidence. A statewide enumeration visited 360,319 homes and identified 187,719 out-of-school children aged six to 17, including 106,353 boys and 81,366 girls. Enumerators used digital devices, geofencing and independent checks. The result was a name-and-location map showing where excluded children live and why they are missing school.
That distinction has transformed planning. When the household map is combined with the digital Annual School Census, government can see both sides of the problem: children outside the system and the schools, teachers and classrooms available within it. Kaduna can consequently decide where a new school is essential, where an existing one requires expansion, where teachers are scarce, and where feeding, transport, cash support, community engagement or a flexible calendar will achieve more than another building. Reform becomes precise rather than performative.
The map also dismantles comfortable generalisations. Kaduna North Senatorial Zone carries about half of the identified burden, but exclusion differs sharply among communities. Kubau’s problem is strongly connected to shortages within the education system. In Giwa, farm labour exerts a powerful pull on children. Makarfi requires stronger post-primary and vocational pathways. Soba demands deeper cultural and community engagement, while poverty and displacement weigh heavily in Igabi. A uniform remedy would waste resources; evidence permits the administration to match each barrier with an appropriate response.
Other findings are equally instructive. Nearly two-thirds of excluded children are of primary-school age, proving that intervention must begin at the point of first enrolment. More than 60 per cent have never attended school, while the remainder entered and later dropped out, often during the earliest primary years. These groups require different solutions: mobilisation and first-time access for one, recovery and accelerated re-entry for the other. More than 17,000 children have spent over two years outside education, increasing the urgency of catch-up programmes.
The data has also exposed a gender reversal that policy must not ignore. Boys constitute 56.7 per cent of the identified population, influenced significantly by farming, petty commerce and informal apprenticeships. Protecting girl-child education remains indispensable, but the evidence now requires an equally deliberate boy-child retention strategy. It is precisely this willingness to follow facts rather than stereotypes that gives the Kaduna model its national importance. The federal government’s decision to embrace the household-mapping approach as a framework for wider identification validates a notable subnational innovation: Kaduna is not merely responding to a national crisis; it is helping Nigeria rethink how that crisis should be measured.
The movement from an estimated out-of-school population of about 535,000 at the beginning of the Governor Sani administration to a directly enumerated 187,719 is profoundly encouraging, although the figures arise from different methods and age parameters and should not be treated as a strict statistical comparison.
The responsible conclusion is nevertheless compelling. Kaduna has moved from broad estimates exceeding half a million to a verified register of fewer than 200,000 children, while interventions have returned large numbers to learning. The achievement deserves celebration, but the remaining 187,719 children constitute an obligation, not a footnote.
Behind this machinery is the ROOSC Project Management Unit coordinated by Mr Ezra Angai. Under his leadership the Project has been a huge success. Angai’s background in banking, development work and public administration equips him for that demanding intersection. Under his stewardship, the unit has translated the governor’s policy direction into implementation, monitoring resources and results across communities while keeping the project centred on measurable outcomes.
His coordination has helped make ROOSC one of the administration’s most persuasive demonstrations of placing capable hands in critical positions. The project’s emerging success belongs to a wider chain of leadership: a governor who established the priority and defended the investment; education institutions that convert policy into service; partners that provide finance and expertise; teachers who animate classrooms; communities that release and support their children; and a management team that holds the parts together. Effective reform is rarely the work of one office, but it always requires leadership able to give many offices a common purpose.
Governor Sani’s education record is ultimately a statement about the kind of Kaduna he seeks to build. Every child returned to school is one life less exposed to illiteracy, exploitation, criminal recruitment, forced marriage and inherited poverty. Every competent teacher retained, classroom restored and meal served strengthens not only an education system but the social foundations of peace. The long-term value of ROOSC will therefore exceed its enrolment figures, because education enlarges productive citizenship and gives vulnerable communities a stake in stability.
The work is unfinished. Insecurity still closes schools and displaces families. Poverty still forces impossible choices. Teacher shortages, infrastructure gaps, early dropout and social resistance remain formidable. But Kaduna now possesses what serious reform requires: political commitment, remarkably improved security conditions across the state, substantial financing, household-level evidence, differentiated interventions and accountable coordination. It has moved beyond lamenting the out-of-school crisis to building an instrument capable of defeating it.
That is the significance of the Sani education story. It is the story of reform graduating into results, of public expenditure acquiring a human face, and of excluded children becoming visible to the state by name, location and need. Through ROOSC, ably coordinated by Ezra Angai, Kaduna has shown that the scourge of out-of-school children is neither inevitable nor beyond remedy. It can be reduced when compassion is organised, resources are protected and policy is governed by evidence.
The most fitting tribute to the Governor Sani administration is therefore found not in rhetoric, but in the growing number of Kaduna children walking back into classrooms; and towards futures once placed beyond their reach.
•Kubau, a freelance journalist, resides in Kurmin Mashi, Kaduna.

title: Lack of volunteers sees Pride events cancelled in regional WA
content:
Low volunteer numbers see pride events cancelled in regional WA, but there is one bright spot
Organisers of queer festivals in regional Western Australia say their events are at risk of vanishing due to a lack of people willing to help coordinate every year, as another Pride parade bites the dust.
In Carnarvon, about 900 kilometres north of Perth, those pressures have brought the town's 2026 parade to an end after three years, despite being well supported in the community.
Most of the committee behind Queernarvon has stepped down or moved away, leaving the group without enough volunteers.
In the state's south, Busselton's long-running Pride parade has also been cancelled, with organisers instead directing their limited resources towards education and wellbeing events.
But in the Pilbara, a Pride festival that began as a small games night among friends has grown to attract about 1,500 people, with organisers crediting support from the wider community for its success.
So, what are the obstacles for LGTBIQA+ people living in the regions?
Changing views
Queernarvon chair Carmen Reilly said Pride events played an important role in regional communities.
In her view, there had been a shift in public perception towards trans, gender diverse and young LGBTQI+ people.
"I have had several conversations over the last few months with people who have never met a trans person, but have seen posts and AI clips on social media and have formed their opinions," she said.
"I say to those people, 'If you're basing your opinions and ideas on social media, put the phone down, go out and meet someone who has a different life experience to you.'"
She said events such as these helped build real connections within communities.
"There's more connecting us than dividing us,"she said.
Finding a community
Johnathan Trace, who is working in Carnarvon on a holiday visa, said he made the decision to leave his home country of the United States because the rise of the far right made him feel unsafe as a trans man.
"I was like, 'It's time. I need to get out of here,'" he said.
Since being in Australia, Mr Trace said he had felt safer but still experienced moments that made him feel unsafe and unwelcome.
Those ranged from nasty comments delivered by strangers in the bathroom, to homophobic outbursts from customers he was serving at work.
Mr Trace said it was a shame the Carnarvon event was cancelled, as there were a lack of spaces to discuss his life experiences as a trans man.
"You're surrounded by all these backpackers who are just here for a good time, who don't want to talk about politics or anything that ruins their good vibes," Mr Trace said.
"It's very hard to find a real community where you can talk about your queerness and the negative things you face with that."
Mining towns lead the way
A bright spot for WA Pride celebrations is in the state's mining region.
The Pilbara Pride Festival started from a small games night among friends, but is now in its fifth year, with about 1,500 people estimated to attend the events across places such as Port Hedland, Karratha and Onslow.
Port Hedland Lesbian, Allies, Gays Society (PHLAGS+) secretary Gloria Jacob put the success down to dedicated volunteers and support from local government and the resources sector.
"This year in particular, the one thing that filled my cup was the high school students asking us to hold a workshop at the school, and the high school allowing us to do that," Ms Jacob said.
But she said it had not always been this way.
"I can tell you there were times in the early days where it wasn't that pleasant, and it still isn't pleasant," she said.
"But the main reason we do it is to ensure our young people, our First Nations people and those who are less able to access these safe spaces know PHLAGS+ exist."
'Space to be themselves'
A local church initially protested against the PHLAGS+ Pride events.
"But the second year they actually marched with us in the parade," Ms Jacob said.
"The more people engage and the more people become aware — it becomes the norm."
Ms Jacob said if support was not upheld by the wider community, the regions will lose their diversity.
"If they don't feel like they are welcome or supported or have space to be themselves openly, you're going to lose them to the city,"she said.
"The city can be brought to the communities, we've proven it through Pilbara Pride."

title: Dr Te Ripowai Higgins: An unrelenting champion of te ao Māori
content:
"Mō tēnei hōnore i homaihia nei, kei au te waimarie, nā te mea i a au e tipu mai ana e patua ana i te kura mō te kōrero i tō tātou reo. Ka mutu, koirā anake te reo i mōhio mātou."
Recognition like this is poignant, especially considering I was among the generations beaten at school for speaking our language, it's the only language we knew.
- Dr Te Ripowai Higgins, QSM, ONZM
Beaten for speaking te reo Māori at school, Dr Te Ripowai Higgins (Ngāi Tūhoe) dedicated her career to keeping her language and culture alive.
Her relentless dedication to a language she was punished for speaking has been recognised by the Governor-General at an investiture ceremony this week, where she received the Officer of the New Zealand Order of Merit (ONZM) for more than 43 years of service to education and Māori.
Dr Higgins reflected on the acknowledgement and shared her thoughts with Pūkāea.
"Mō tēnei hōnore i homaihia nei, kei au te waimarie, nā te mea i a au e tipu mai ana e patua ana i te kura mō te kōrero i tō tātou reo. Ka mutu, koirā anake te reo i mōhio mātou."
I find this type of recognition quite poignant, especially considering I was among the generations beaten at school for speaking our native tongue.
The assimilationist education system of the time prioritised English and contributed to the suppression and decline of te reo Māori.
But the punishment had the opposite effect on Dr Higgins.
She says kaumātua and kuia taught her generation to withstand those pressures and turn adversity into opportunity.
"Nā rātou i tohu, 'kia kaha koutou, ahakoa patua koutou, me ako koutou i taua reo. Kei te pai tō koutou reo Māori. Kua nui ake ngā Pākehā e haere mai ana, me ako koutou i tā rātou ake reo, kia mōhio ake tātou kei te aha ngā kōrero'."
They told us not to let the beatings break us; they helped us recognise that learning their language didn't mean we had to abandon our own. They said Pākehā would not stop coming, they told us we had to adapt and master their language so we would always know what they were saying."
The ability to navigate two worlds became a defining feature of Dr Higgins' career.
She went on to help establish initiatives that created pathways for te reo Māori in education, broadcasting and public life.
In 1982, she became a foundation board member of Te Ataarangi, the Māori language revitalisation movement.
She remained involved for 42 years, helping generations learn te reo Māori while sharing the approach with Indigenous communities overseas.
Her influence extended into Māori broadcasting.
She served three terms on the board of Te Māngai Pāho and was instrumental in establishing Te Upoko o te Ika, recognised as Aotearoa's first Māori radio station.
Those initiatives established foundations for the ongoing development of more education and media initiatives dedicated to fostering te reo Māori.
Dr Higgins says her aspiration is to ensure generations to come maintain pride in their identity.
"Karekau e tino aro atu ana ki ngā tohu pēnei. Ko te āhua kei te tino hiahia kia kitea, ko te whakakaha ake i te nui o ngā tāngata e kōrero Māori ana, heoi i tū atu I te reo, kia whakatauira ai rātou i te mana me te mōhio o ngā kuia, kaumātua."
Things like this have never interested me. The work I have done over the years is focussed on supporting the establishment of initiatives that encourage Māori to embrace their language, beyond that. I want future generations to take pride in their identity and represent their culture with integrity, I hope they, like me aspire to make their kaumātua and kuia proud."
Dr Higgins' daughter, Dr Rawinia Higgins is demonstrating the impact of her mother's work through her own role as Māori Language Commissioner, helping lead the revitalisation of te reo Māori.
Speaking to Radio New Zealand about the importance of Te wiki o Te Reo Māori, Higgins said the growing number of people learning the language is encouraging, and the commission's rangahau (research) continues to show that many New Zealanders see te reo Māori as a valuable part of the country's identity.
"This is a three generation kaupapa," she said.
"Every little step that each generation takes is really important."

title: Outback town marks 60th anniversary of plane crash that claimed 24 lives
content:
Winton remembers deadly Ansett-ANA Flight 149 crash 60 years on
In short:
Ansett-ANA Flight 149 crashed near the outback Queensland town of Winton on September 22nd 1966, killing all 24 people aboard.
The crash triggered one of the largest aviation investigations in Australia's history.
As the Winton community and loved ones of those who died pay their respects, the daughter of one of the pilots continues to work on an oral history project to document the crash and its fallout.
Sixty years ago, what was meant to be a short flight between two Western Queensland towns ended in one of Australia's deadliest aviation crashes.
Conditions were favourable when Ansett-ANA Flight 149 took off from Mount Isa, bound for Brisbane via Longreach, on September 22, 1966.
But 30 minutes into the flight an engine was on fire and the aircraft was put into an emergency descent before breaking apart in the air and crashing onto a cattle property 19 kilometres west of Winton.
All 24 people on board died.
As the small outback community nearly 200 kilometres north-west of Longreach gathered to mark the 60th anniversary, they remembered the lives that were lost and the impact the tragedy had on the aviation industry.
Community mourns
Winton Mayor Cathy White said the crash greatly affected the community.
"Sixty years on, there are people here that remember it like it happened yesterday," she said.
"I think we should always come and remember [together]."
At the ceremony on Tuesday locals and the families of those who died paid their respects.
Elizabeth Gillam, the daughter of co-pilot John Gillam, was 18 months old when her father died.
"It was a defining feature of my life," she said.
"When the crash happened, my mum went from being a stay-at-home mum to being the breadwinner, so everything changed."
Dr Gillam said it was important to hear the stories of other people affected.
"All of these families, all of these people in the Winton community were brought together by this one singular event," she said.
"So many lives were changed."
Anne O'Leary's father, Ken Cooper, piloted the plane.
She said his loss significantly changed the dynamic of her family's life. Her mum had no choice but to go to work and the family home was sold to make ends meet.
Ms O'Leary said her two younger brothers followed in their dad's footsteps and became pilots themselves.
"I became a teacher. My older brother and I do not like to fly, but we do manage that," she said.
Ms O'Leary attended the 25th anniversary, which she said was "cathartic and gave them closure".
"After 60 years it's more about meeting other people, sharing stories and dedicating the memory to them," she said.
Extensive investigation
The tragedy led to one of the largest aviation crash investigation in Australian history.
State Library of New South Wales historian Peter Hobbins said the Air Safety Investigation Branch (the predecessor to the Australian Transport Safety Bureau) launched an investigation and the federal government ordered an independent inquiry.
"[It] ended up costing the Commonwealth an estimated $1.12 million, in 1967 terms," he said.
Dr Hobbins said the investigation and the following independent inquiry concluded that a small "blower" motor that helped deliver air into the cabin had worn out and caught fire, also igniting one of the engines.
That caused parts of the plane to melt before the wing broke off, tearing the roof open on descent.
Dr Hobbins said the crash attracted the attention it did because there had been two other similar crashes in Australia that decade.
"I think to have an accident as severe as the one at Winton pushed hard against that sense of comfort that Australians were starting to assume about airline travel," he said.
Dr Hobbins said the inquiry drove home the need for better monitoring and servicing intervals, and that the investigation reinforced Australia's dedication to becoming a world leader in aviation safety.
"For the last nearly 60 years, it actually has been incredibly safe," he said.
"I think a lot of the roots of that [safety] culture were set in the 1950s and the 1960s."
Documenting oral history
Dr Gillam believes there are lessons to be learned from the crash and has spent the last decade working to document them.
After the 50th anniversary she started an oral history project to collect testimonies from anyone who remembered the days and weeks following the tragedy.
As part of that research Dr Gillam spoke with investigator Don Wally.
"He was able to explain in great detail what had happened," she said.
Dr Gillam's project is ongoing and she is keen to speak with other people who have been affected, not just to capture what happened on that day in 1966, but to learn more about the wider ramifications, including how the families were compensated in the aftermath.
"All of these are important to capture, for history, to work out how we can do things better."

title: Tribes hit hard by wildfires face health effects, cultural losses
content:
Nada Hassanein
Stateline
Neighbors across the Colville Tribes communities in Washington state knew Matilda Bob’s log home as the “rainbow house,” for its brightly painted exterior.
Now it’s gone.
Sparked by a lightning strike in mid-July, the Kaiser Canyon Fire destroyed Bob’s home and 42 other houses on the Colville Reservation, along with 100 outbuildings such as sheds and barns, tribal leaders said.
“I couldn’t believe that it had happened,” said Bob. “It went so fast.”
Tribal leaders across Washington and Oregon told Stateline that this year’s record-breaking wildfires burned timber that they rely on for income, threatened food sources and waterways, and harmed the health of their communities. Power outages left families without food they’ve hunted or gathered and frozen.
Hotter, drier conditions driven by climate change already have made wildfires nationwide more frequent and intense, a trend that is expected to accelerate. Substandard housing and higher rates of acute and chronic underlying health conditions, including respiratory illnesses, make tribal communities more vulnerable during and after the fires.
“What typically used to be like a two-month fire season for us when I first started fighting fire about 25 years ago — now that’s at least three months and sometimes longer, depending on the year,” said Cody Desautel, executive director of the Colville Tribes, who is also a forester and wildland fire expert.
An especially warm winter also left Washington state with about half its usual snowpack, raising drought concerns and wildfire risks.
This year saw particularly devastating fires in eastern Washington, including arson-instigated fires that destroyed over 700 homes in Spokane. The conditions prompted Washington state Democratic Gov. Bob Ferguson to declare a statewide state of emergency on Aug. 1, citing an “unprecedented” red flag alert of extreme fire danger from the National Weather Service.
The Colville Reservation includes the southern portion of Ferry County, which has the second-lowest median household income of all counties in the state. The tribe lost a significant amount of timber, a main source of income, during the fires.
Many residents didn’t have home insurance because the housing didn’t qualify or they couldn’t afford it, said Cindy Marchand, chairwoman of the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation, adding that about half of homes destroyed in the fires weren’t insured. Other residents couldn’t afford to upgrade to more fire-resistant material, she said.
“The rates are just astronomical in the sense that a lot of people in our area are not able to afford this,” Marchand said. “We have elders living on a single income, they’re on a fixed income, and so they’re having a hard time making it as it is.”
By mid-September, the total acres burned across the state reached roughly 900,000 acres, the worst since 2015.
Since July, about 200,000 acres burned across the Colville Reservation alone, with the Kaiser Canyon Fire scorching over 138,000 acres and the Modrite fire burning more than 57,000 acres.
In Oregon, over 60,000 acres burned across the reservation of the Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs, where at least six homes were destroyed.
The Wrights Spring Fire in Oregon burned through 55,000 acres across Klamath County, national forest and tribal lands.
Health effects
Faith Zacherle-Tonasket has seen how the wildfires have affected perinatal health. Founder of xa?xa? Indigenous Birth Justice, which offers perinatal and doula support across the Colville Reservation, Zacherle-Tonasket said three of her clients went into early labor during this year’s fires. She and her team believe stress amid displacement due to evacuations contributed to the early labor. Emerging research is also showing how wildfire smoke is a primary pollutant affecting pregnancy.
Zacherle-Tonasket also helps lead the River Warrior Society, a nonprofit offering wildfire relief for tribal and non-tribal members. The group has been coordinating shelter placements for elders, donations and food assistance.
“This is one of the biggest fires our reservation has had,” she said. “The biggest need we have on our reservation is air purifiers.”
Respiratory health has been a major concern post-wildfires amid smoke and poor air quality. American Indian and Alaska Native people disproportionately have chronic respiratory health conditions exacerbated by wildfire smoke, including asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Matilda Bob’s father, a veteran who is now displaced with her, has COPD.
Along with respiratory distress, there’s been “tremendous stress, anxiety, grief, trauma — and we expect and know that those behavioral health needs are going to continue beyond this current emergency. Post-fire recovery creates additional health concerns,” said Dayna Seymour, the Colville Tribes’ health and human services chair. “Our members are going in now to clean up the ash and debris, and aren’t really always sure what’s in that ash and debris, whether there’s hazardous materials, heavy metals, asbestos or other contaminants.”
Seymour added that community members helped deliver medications to their displaced neighbors and helped each other dig fire lines.
Research shows disproportionate smoke exposure among tribes in California, noted University of Kansas Assistant Professor Melinda Adams, a cultural fire practitioner and scholar who teaches in the Department of Earth, Energy, and Environment.
“Because wildfire is increasing in frequency and intensity,” said Adams, a member of the N’dee San Carlos Apache Tribe of Arizona, “we must look at cumulative effects and identify patterns in human and environmental health while investing in climate and wildfire mitigation strategies that include Indigenous knowledge.”
Prescribed burns, carefully controlled fires to reduce brush that could fuel megablazes, are crucial tools in preventing dangerous wildfires and preserving ecosystem health. But regulatory barriers have made implementing traditional Indigenous burn practices difficult, Desautel and Adams said.
This week, the U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee advanced legislation that would streamline approval of prescribed burns, while the EPA issued guidance last year.
Funding and staffing limitations are also a barrier, Desautel added. The Indian Forest Management Assessment Team found that Indian trust forest lands are funded at about a third per acre of comparable federal forests.
Waterway pollution, cultural art lost
Seymour added that traditional foods including huckleberries and herbs and roots, such as bitterroot and camas, that the tribes rely on were scorched across the land.
“Those are things that we utilize to help us in ceremony, that we utilize to eat for subsistence. So that was a huge loss for our people,” Seymour said.
In Oregon, while no homes were lost on the Klamath Tribes’ lands, leaders still have concerns and uncertainty around environmental aftereffects, particularly on traditional food systems the tribes were finally in the process of regenerating.
The tribes had just started restoring their ancestral salmon after removal of four dams two years ago. Last year, the tribes documented the first adult Chinook salmon in the Williamson River, and earlier this year detected the first salmon hatch in over a century in the tributaries of the Upper Klamath Lake.
“The biggest (wildfire) impact is the effects on hunting and gathering that may be felt in the future. …With this high-intensity, high-severity wildfire, there’s likelihood of sedimentation into the streams that could serve as spawning grounds for that new salmon,” said Tim Sexton, Wildland Fire Program Manager at the Klamath Tribes. Research is showing how wildfires affect fish habitats.
Klamath Tribes Chairman William Ray Jr., a former firefighter of 40 years, said he’s been advocating for tribal control of the waterways amid pollution that already existed before this year’s wildfires.
“We have ecological collapse going on. Our water quality in our lake and rivers isn’t very good,” he said.
At the Colville Reservation, Zacherle-Tonasket said many of her community members are holding off on traditional hunting and instead her nonprofit has gotten discounts from local butchers to help families.
“We don’t want to hunt this year,” she told Stateline. “It’s just ethically not right to hunt when our own animals are suffering the way we are.”
Bob said that many cultural heirlooms burned — her own traditional beadwork, a 100-year-old berry basket passed down from her great grandmother, and her nephew’s handmade attire worn during special dances at powwows.
But her family will continue to dance as they do “for the people who can’t,” she said, on their ancestral land.
“Every time your foot hits the floor’s a prayer,” she said. “We were raised to respect the land. … We’re still standing in the fact that we’re all OK, that we all made it, that we didn’t lose anybody.”
Stateline reporter Nada Hassanein can be reached at nhassanein@stateline.org.

title: Accessible Technology for Hope: Bridging Gaps with Innovative Tools
content:
Accessible technology for hope is transforming lives by removing barriers that have long kept people with disabilities from full participation in society. At Global Positive News Network, we believe that innovation in digital tools isn’t just about convenience-it’s about fundamental human dignity and equal opportunity.
The solutions emerging today are real, practical, and already making measurable differences in employment, education, and independence. This blog post explores how these innovations work and what comes next in building a truly inclusive digital world.
How Accessible Technology Creates Real Opportunity
Removing Barriers That Block Daily Life
Accessible technology works because it removes specific, concrete barriers that people with disabilities face every day. A person who is blind can navigate websites and applications through screen readers that convert text to speech, allowing them to apply for jobs, manage finances, and access educational content independently. According to the American Foundation for the Blind, screen reader users have access to properly configured digital tools that support workplace inclusion. Voice recognition technology has advanced significantly, with tools like Google Assistant and Apple’s Siri achieving 95% accuracy rates in understanding speech commands, enabling people with mobility limitations to control computers, smartphones, and smart home devices without touching a keyboard or mouse. These aren’t theoretical improvements-they translate directly into people working, learning, and living without constant dependence on others.
Employment Gains Through Accessible Design
The employment impact is measurable and substantial. The World Health Organization reports that people with disabilities experience unemployment rates nearly double those of people without disabilities, yet accessible technology supports an estimated 1.3 billion people who experience significant disability globally. When employers implement proper accessibility features like adjustable font sizes, customizable color schemes, and keyboard navigation options, they tap into this talent pool. Companies like Microsoft and IBM have reported that accessible hiring practices increased their qualified applicant pools by 30% or more, while simultaneously improving retention rates.
Education and Independence Through Technology
Educational access has expanded equally-online learning platforms with captions, transcripts, and adjustable playback speeds enable deaf and hard-of-hearing students to participate fully in courses. Research from the National Association of the Deaf shows that captioned videos improve comprehension for all learners by an average of 15%. Independence grows when technology adapts to individual needs rather than forcing people to adapt to rigid systems. This shift from one-size-fits-all design to personalized, flexible interfaces represents a fundamental change in how we build digital tools.
The real power of accessible technology lies not in its complexity but in its practical results. People with disabilities gain control over their own lives, employers access wider talent pools, and educational institutions reach more students effectively. These outcomes depend on continued innovation and widespread adoption of accessibility standards across industries. Understanding what innovations currently exist sets the stage for examining the tools and technologies that are already reshaping possibilities for millions of people worldwide.
What Technology Powers Accessibility Today
Voice Assistants Transform Daily Control
AI-powered voice assistants have become the most practical entry point for accessibility because they work across devices and require minimal setup. Google Assistant, Apple’s Siri, and Amazon’s Alexa now handle complex commands with 95% accuracy rates, allowing people with mobility or visual impairments to control computers, phones, and smart home systems without keyboards or touchscreens. These tools work in real homes and workplaces right now, not in laboratories. A person with severe arthritis can dictate emails, schedule appointments, and navigate applications entirely through speech, eliminating the physical strain that previously forced many out of the workforce. The National Federation of the Blind reports that voice-controlled devices have become an increasingly adopted accessibility solution by people with disabilities.
Screen Readers Enable Workplace Productivity
Screen readers remain the backbone of web and application accessibility, converting digital text into audio output that blind users can navigate at their own pace. NVDA, a free open-source screen reader, has become standard in education and many workplaces because it costs nothing and works reliably across Windows systems. JAWS, a commercial alternative, costs around $1,200 but offers advanced features for complex professional software. The difference between these tools and older solutions matters significantly-speed and accuracy directly impact productivity. A 2024 WebAIM study found that screen readers enable blind employees to work effectively in professional environments, with adoption of tools like VoiceOver growing significantly among users with disabilities.
Natural-Sounding Speech Technology
Text-to-speech technology has improved dramatically beyond robotic-sounding voices, with natural-sounding options now available through tools like Natural Reader and Read&Write. These solutions integrate directly into Microsoft Office and Google Workspace, making them workplace standards that employers must provide to comply with accessibility regulations in most developed countries. The shift from specialized software to integrated tools means organizations can support accessibility without expensive separate purchases.
Adaptive Hardware and Built-In System Features
Physical accessibility requires both hardware adaptation and software flexibility working together. Customizable keyboards with programmable keys, eye-tracking devices that translate eye movement into cursor control, and switch-activated systems that respond to single button presses have all become more affordable and powerful. Tobii’s eye-tracking technology, once limited to research settings, now costs under $400 for consumer versions and integrates with Windows 10 and 11 natively.
The real innovation lies in how operating systems now support these devices. Windows Accessibility Settings and macOS Accessibility features allow users to adjust font sizes, increase color contrast, enable high-contrast modes, and remap keyboard functions without purchasing specialized software.
This shift toward built-in accessibility means a person with low vision can make a computer usable within minutes instead of spending hundreds on dedicated adaptive technology. Organizations worldwide have recognized this trend, making accessibility a standard feature rather than an afterthought.
These technological advances have created the foundation for broader change. Yet technology alone cannot sustain progress-the organizations, policies, and communities that champion accessibility standards determine whether these innovations reach the people who need them most.
Who’s Making Accessibility Happen Right Now
Tech Giants Embed Accessibility Into Core Products
Microsoft and Apple have embedded accessibility into their core product development rather than treating it as an afterthought, which fundamentally changes what gets built. Microsoft’s Accessibility Insights tool works publicly and free, allowing developers to test websites and applications for accessibility compliance without expensive audits. Apple’s commitment shows in concrete numbers: iOS supports over 20 accessibility features built directly into the operating system, from VoiceOver to Switch Control, meaning users don’t need to purchase separate adaptive technology. These represent actual engineering resources and product roadmap decisions that prioritize disabled users from the beginning of development.
Regulations Transform Accessibility Into Business Requirements
The European Union’s Web Accessibility Directive, which took effect in 2020, requires all public sector websites and applications to meet WCAG 2.1 AA standards or face legal consequences. This regulatory pressure has forced organizations across Europe to invest in accessibility compliance, creating demand for accessible design expertise and pushing vendors to build accessible products as standard features. The Americans with Disabilities Act’s digital accessibility requirements produce similar effects in the United States, though enforcement remains inconsistent. Countries like Canada and Australia have followed with their own standards, meaning multinational organizations now find it simpler to build accessible products globally than to maintain separate accessible and inaccessible versions.
This regulatory shift matters because it transforms accessibility from a nice-to-have feature into a business requirement with financial consequences for non-compliance. Organizations ignoring these standards face lawsuits-Target paid $6 million in 2008 for website accessibility violations, and similar cases continue today, making accessibility a liability issue that finance departments finally understand.
Disability Advocates Hold Companies Accountable
Grassroots momentum comes from disability advocacy organizations that test products, publish accessibility ratings, and hold companies accountable. The National Federation of the Blind publishes accessibility scorecards for major technology companies, directly influencing purchasing decisions by government agencies and large employers. Disabled people themselves have become accessibility auditors and consultants, moving beyond passive users to active participants in product design. Companies like Deque Systems now employ disabled professionals specifically to audit accessibility, recognizing that disabled people understand accessibility barriers better than non-disabled designers ever will. This shift from consultation to employment of disabled people in accessibility roles has accelerated progress because it embeds lived experience into product decisions rather than relying on theoretical guidelines.
Final Thoughts
Accessible technology for hope has moved from concept to reality, with screen readers, voice assistants, and adaptive devices now serving as working tools that people depend on daily for employment, education, and independence. Employers who implement accessibility features report 30% increases in qualified applicants, while educational platforms with captions improve comprehension for all learners by 15%. Regulatory standards like the EU’s Web Accessibility Directive have transformed accessibility from optional to mandatory, forcing meaningful change across industries and proving that progress happens when organizations prioritize disabled people in product design.
Technology companies must continue embedding accessibility into core products rather than treating it as an afterthought, and governments need consistent enforcement of existing standards alongside stronger regulations. Organizations that hire disabled people as accessibility consultants and product designers gain competitive advantages because lived experience drives better solutions than external expertise alone. Companies that build accessible products access wider talent pools and customer bases while societies that prioritize accessibility benefit from fuller participation of disabled people in economic and civic life.
This isn’t charity-it’s recognizing that accessibility benefits everyone while creating fundamental fairness. Those wanting to learn more about accessible solutions and stories of positive change can visit Global Positive News Network for curated content on community impact and human progress, including accessibility initiatives making real differences worldwide.
