title: After two failed bids, Ipswich remains hopeful of becoming an NRL side
content:
Rugby league has a storied history in Ipswich, and local clubs are pushing for it to become home to the next NRL side.
The Ipswich Jets first made a bid to join the league 16 years ago.
The city's bid is facing strong competition from the Christchurch-based Southern Orcas.
After almost two decades and two failed bids, rugby league diehards in Ipswich are once again dreaming of a place in the NRL.
The league's 20th team is expected to be announced by the end of the year, with the Queensland city's bid facing strong competition from the Christchurch-based Southern Orcas.
"We don't underestimate the fight on our hands," Rugby League Ipswich Chairman David Nugent said.
"[But] don't underestimate an Ipswich person in a fight, we'll give it our all."
Rugby league has been inseparable from the cultural identity of the former coal-mining city since the early 20th century.
It takes hold of people early, often passed down through generations.
David Haug is a perfect example. At the North Ipswich Tigers clubhouse, it's easier to name what he hasn't done at the club.
"I've played since I was under nines … coached everything from under sevens through to A-grade, been on the committee and done everything from committee member to president," he said.
That tends to be how it goes in the former industrial city west of Brisbane.
Here the game takes hold early, often carried through generations.
Ipswich's community sports fields have been a consistent breeding ground of rugby league players.
From Dud Beattie in the 1950s, to Allan "Alfie" Langer in the 1990s, and Broncos NRLW captain Ali Brigginshaw today.
But none have been able to represent their home city at the top level.
"[Ipswich players] get to a certain age … and then get picked up by other Sydney clubs and they don't get a chance to actually come back and play for their city," Mr Haug said.
Player factory
It was this exodus of talent that sparked the first Western Corridor bid in 2010, which also included the Darling Downs city of Toowoomba.
"Our young kids were leaving home at 16 to live their rugby league dreams … and for every 10 that went down the Pacific Highway, nine came back with broken hearts," Ipswich Jets chair Steve Johnson said.
But Mr Johnson, who is spearheading the bid, believes the benefits of the Jets becoming the league's 20th team would spread far beyond Ipswich.
"With the expansion at the moment with PNG and Western Australia, [the NRL] needs more players and we will surely generate more players than we need."
"We'll become a player factory for the entire NRL."
University of Technology Sydney Sports Economics Professor Tim Harcourt said new clubs generally had to bring two things to the NRL: spectators and TV viewers.
"It's definitely rugby league heartland," Mr Harcourt said.
"And secondly, it's attractive economically to have more Brisbane derbies in a sense, because you'll have the Dolphins and Broncos, and then I guess the Jets."
But he believed the Ipswich bid's biggest competitor, the Christchurch-based Southern Orcas, was in a better position to become the NRL's 20th team.
He said Christchurch would be a more attractive destination for travelling fans, which the NRL would likely take into consideration.
"There's a lot of tourism to the South Island of New Zealand already, with Lord of the Rings and all the beautiful landscape."
"They've also got this brand new stadium which is fantastic for all sorts of sports and events, so they're kind of ready to go," Mr Harcourt said.
With no suitable stadium in Ipswich, the Jets would have to play at Brisbane's Lang Park.
The Jets are hoping to turn North Ipswich Reserve into a 12,000-seat rectangular stadium, but are yet to secure all necessary funding.
Eyes turn to next generation
Far removed from the boardroom machinations at Rugby League Central in Sydney, those who have spent decades working at the grassroots level consider an Ipswich NRL team through the eyes of local under-18s players.
"For me, the driving force is every kid involved in sport is one less kid on the street," Redbank Plains Bears President Jodie Elder said.
"For some kids it just means everything. It could be the highlight of their week to come to training."
Rory Morley-Davies plays for the North Ipswich Tigers under-15s side and started playing football at a young age.
"I don't think any other sport fulfils me like rugby does," he said.
"When [people in Ipswich] think of a sport, they don't think of anything other than rugby league."
"Everyone wouldn't want anything else, except for Ipswich to have a rugby league team, and I think it's a long time coming."

title: Mary Goretti Kariaga: The Kenyan scientist who pioneered mushroom farming in Kenya
content:
Mary Goretti Kariaga: The Kenyan scientist who pioneered mushroom farming in Kenya
What you need to know:
- From plant pathology and sugarcane research to pioneering commercial mushroom production, Mary Goretti Kariaga built a remarkable career in Kenyan science and agriculture.
- Her journey took her from the University of Nairobi to Zimbabwe and back to Kenya, where she pioneered mushroom farming and trained aspiring growers.
On August 1, 1982, Mary Goretti Kariaga was in her third trimester of pregnancy with her first child when intense anxiety took hold of her. She was in her rented house in Arina, Kisumu, listening to KBC news of an emerging coup. She grew more worried as she wondered whether hospitals would be operational in time for her delivery.
Mary's father, John Joseph Odera, a successful entrepreneur, valued academic advancement. He funded her O-Levels at Loreto Girls in Limuru and her A-Levels at Kenya High School, instilling in her a strong drive for intellectual achievement. She enrolled at the University of Nairobi in 1975 and graduated four years later with a Bachelor of Education (Science).
She was recruited as an Agricultural Research Officer at the Kenya Agricultural Research Institute in Kibos, Kisumu. After the attempted coup, Mary safely delivered her first child, Patricia, on the night of August 17, 1982, at Kisumu's Victoria Hospital. She later travelled to Port Louis to spend three months at the Mauritius Sugar Industry Institute, studying the agronomy of sugarcane cultivation.
In 1986, she began her master's degree in plant pathology at the University of Nairobi, focusing on fungal, bacterial and nematode diseases. Her thesis centred on parasitic nematodes of sugar cane, and she later authored an academic manual titled Plant Parasitic Nematodes Associated with Sugar Cane at the Nyanza Sugar Belt. She also looked into the challenges of communal sugarcane farming and completed her studies in 1988, a year before giving birth to her son, Stephen.
She became a member of African Women in Science and Engineering, an associate of the International Network of Women Engineers and Scientists, and a founding scholar of the Kenya Professional Association of Women in Agriculture and Environment. Her expertise led to her appointment at the Lake Basin Development Authority's Fibre Research Station in Kibos.
In 1995, she began lecturing at Maseno University before moving with her family to Harare, Zimbabwe, on January 5, 1999, after her husband, Billy, was employed by the University of Zimbabwe. Her deep interest in fungi led her to start a botanical programme to study mushroom cultivation. She began culturing and bulking spawn (mushroom seeds), and in 2000, she started producing Agaricus bisporus (button mushrooms) at the secondary entrance to her home, at the back of the University of Zimbabwe campus.
Also read: Kabete's queen of mushroom farming
Mary held weekend mushroom training sessions for interested participants at her house and went on to study the production of other edible mushrooms, including Ganoderma lucidum, shiitake and Pleurotus ostreatus (oyster mushrooms).
In September 2001, she walked into Standard Chartered Bank on Bond Street at the Mount Pleasant Shopping Centre, within walking distance of the university. Suddenly, five armed men carrying AK-47 rifles rushed into the bank and ordered the crowd in Shona, "Vese rarai pasi! (Everybody lie down!).”
Because of the similarities between Shona and Swahili, both Bantu languages, Mary understood the order and lay face-down along with the other clients. An overweight white client appeared stunned and confused by the Shona commands until a rifle was pointed directly at his face. Because of his large belly, he ended up lying on his back instead of his stomach, while a terrified woman lying next to Mary began sobbing as the robbers collected money from the tellers.
In her book, The Woman Who Pioneered Mushroom Production in Kenya, Mary writes that minutes after the gunmen left with their loot, everyone remained frozen on the floor in fear. When a person walked in and whispered, “They've gone,” Mary was the first to get up and run out of the bank.
In 2002, she relocated to Kisumu, applied for a position at Maseno's Faculty of Botany, and began pursuing her long-term goal of fighting protein deficiency and raising income levels through mushroom production.
At the time, there were no individual commercial mushroom producers in Kenya. Mary set out to introduce mushroom farming to empower smallholder farmers using oyster mushrooms, which were highly resistant to infection, in high demand and had significant medicinal value.
Because of the uniqueness of her work in mushroom cultivation, Maseno called on her on July 29, 2004, to deliver the keynote presentation to President Mwai Kibaki at the annual Kisumu Agricultural Show. That morning, Kibaki, First Lady Lucy and their security detail listened in astonishment as Mary gave a compelling address on the potential of mushroom production.
Her passion caught the attention of KTN reporter David Ohito, who arranged an interview with Mary and filed a story with his colleague, sparking demand for mushrooms across Kenya. Mary began receiving calls from entrepreneurs requesting mushroom training, as interest in mushroom cultivation grew. She registered her company, Mount Pleasant Mushroom Consultants, named after her former residential suburb in Zimbabwe, and used it to partner different organisations.
She was later elected treasurer of the Universities' Academic Staff Union and negotiated a 50 per cent salary increment for lecturers during the 2007 nationwide strike, the highest lecturers' salary increment in Kenya's history.
In late 2007, Mary's research in sugarcane diseases caught the interest of the Faculty of Agriculture, Veterinary Science and Technology at Masinde Muliro University in Kakamega. She joined the institution and completed her PhD dissertation on Rice Blast, identifying a sequence of four races of the same pathogen, which were later registered at the National Centre for Biotechnology Information. Shortly after being promoted to senior lecturer at Masinde Muliro, she narrowly survived a harrowing carjacking at gunpoint at the entrance of her home.
The writer is a novelist, Big Brother Africa 2 Kenyan representative and founder of Jeff's Fitness Centre (@jeffbigbrother).

title: Tamil Nadu's 70-YO Palmyra Tree Climbers Find New Income Through a Professor's Tourism Trails
content: As the sun rises over the dry stretches of southern Tamil Nadu, silhouettes begin appearing against rows of towering palm trees. Some carry ropes coiled around their shoulders. Others carry sickles and woven baskets. For generations, these climbers have scaled palmyra trees before dawn, tapping sap, harvesting fruit, and collecting leaves that would eventually become everything from jaggery and handicrafts to sweets and roof coverings. Today, many of them are in their seventies. And that worries Dr Preethi Hari Babu. “Without community support, the tree cannot be protected. That is the charm of the palmyra — the community and the tree survive together,” says the 30-year-old tourism researcher and assistant professor from Chennai, whose doctoral research has focused on understanding how Tamil Nadu’s state tree can be revived through tourism and community engagement. “When I understood the benefits of the tree and saw communities trying to revive it, I realised there was so much more to explore,” Dr Preethi says. “I have hosted three tours. In each tour, nearly 20 to 30 people participated. Most of them did not know about the community and their livelihoods. They were overwhelmed to learn about them, purchased the products, and even saved their contacts to place orders in the future,” shares Dr Preethi. A journey that began in a classroom For Preethi, the journey into the world of palmyra did not begin in forests or farms. It began in classrooms. After completing her bachelor’s degree at Ethiraj College and later pursuing an MBA in Tourism, she entered the tourism sector, believing that every place has something unique that shapes its identity. While working with a nature conservation NGO in 2019, she joined a trail focused on palmyra landscapes. That changed everything. “When I understood the benefits of the tree and saw communities trying to revive it, I realised there was so much more to explore,” she says. Eventually, while pursuing her PhD in Tourism from Mizoram University, which she completed in 2025, she turned the palmyra tree into the centre of her research. The idea stayed with her long after the trail ended. Eventually, while pursuing her PhD in Tourism from Mizoram University, which she completed in 2025, she turned the palmyra tree into the centre of her research — not just as a species, but as an ecosystem connecting livelihoods, ecology, culture, and identity. More than just a tree Across Tamil Nadu, palmyra trees stand along roadsides, fields, and coastal landscapes. But according to Preethi, reducing them to scenery misses their significance. Large communities depend on the tree directly for income. “There are edible and non-edible products. There are handicrafts, exports, climbers who harvest products, and women who make jaggery. It creates employment at many levels,” she explains. Large communities depend on the tree directly for income. (Photograph: Gio Shravan) Women’s collectives produce palm jaggery and craft products. Climbers harvest sap and fruit. Artisans weave leaves into baskets and utility products. Entrepreneurs make jams, squashes, and sweets from palm fruit. And then there is the environmental role. The tree helps reduce soil erosion, supports water retention, and acts as a habitat for multiple species. In coastal and dry landscapes especially, these ecological functions become critical. “It is not only useful for people. Many species survive because of these landscapes too,” she says. Where livelihoods climb trees During her fieldwork across Kanyakumari, Thoothukudi, and Villupuram, Preethi spent time with climbing communities whose relationship with palmyra stretches across generations. “There are huge climber communities, almost like fishing communities. Their identity and livelihoods are deeply connected to this tree,” she says. One such climber is 32-year-old Anto Brito, whose family has worked with palmyra trees for generations. “My grandfather was a climber, and my father was also in this profession,” he says. “After my studies, I got a job elsewhere, but I did not find satisfaction there. Here, I am physically fit, I am with my family, and I enjoy the work.” But what struck Preethi most was how invisible many of these value chains remain. (Photograph: Gio Shravan) His family remains deeply involved in the palmyra economy. While Anto climbs the trees and harvests sap and fruit, his parents prepare food products made from palmyra produce. Together, they also run two shops that sell handicrafts and food items derived from the tree. But what struck Preethi most was how invisible many of these value chains remain. Many people know palm fruit. Few know how much more exists. From neera-based beverages to jams, squashes, jelly, adhirasam, and paniyaram, communities continue creating products that rarely receive mainstream attention. For climbers like Anto, the work remains seasonal but can provide a meaningful income. Between April and October, he harvests enough sap to produce around two to three kilograms of karupatti (palm jaggery) a day, earning roughly Rs 1,000 daily during the season. “In a day, I climb more than 10 trees,” he says. “During the COVID period, I used to climb nearly 20 trees a day.” One of them was a fruit festival organised with local communities and hosted at Madras School of Social Work, where artisans and producers from Villupuram showcased dishes made from palmyra produce. To change perceptions around palmyra products, Preethi began organising palmyra trails and community events. One of them was a fruit festival organised with local communities and hosted at Madras School of Social Work, where artisans and producers from Villupuram showcased dishes made from palmyra produce. “About 150 people came and tried the food. Many had never tasted these products before,” she says. The moment that changed perspective One experience continues to stay with her. As part of her extended research, Preethi travelled through remote islands in Indonesia for 15 days, studying how communities there interacted with similar palm ecosystems. Instead of feeling distant, it felt familiar. “I was proud that this potential already existed in Tamil Nadu,” she says. Communities there used palm trees for food, crafts, and even musical instruments. “That was when I realised this tree connects communities across Asia. The community involvement travels with the tree.” The benefits are directly shared among the community and supported by the government. For Preethi, it serves as one of the strongest examples of community-based tourism. (Photograph: Gio Shravan) Rote and Sabu are remote islands in Indonesia. They conserve the palmyra — known locally as lontar — in every possible way. “More than conservation, I can say they co-exist with the tree. Sasando is a traditional harp-like musical instrument native to Rote Island, made from lontar. It is considered a symbol of identity, culture, heritage, and pride. You can see its influence everywhere on the island, from heritage monuments to modern décor inspired by its shape. There is even a Sasando-shaped building that serves as the official residence of the Governor of East Nusa Tenggara in Kupang. “Sabu Island is mostly covered with grasslands and lontar palms. The majority of people depend on the tree for their livelihoods. They make intricate handicrafts such as baskets and handbags, while also preserving their traditional products. “Namata village in Sabu has conical lontar-thatched houses, where visitors can observe animist and ancestral worship practices. Visitors can also experience ikat weaving and watch climbers collect sap from the trees, locally called tuak. The area is underdeveloped in terms of infrastructure, amenities, and sanitation facilities, but it is remarkably well-maintained and organised.” The benefits are directly shared among the community and supported by the government. For Preethi, it serves as one of the strongest examples of community-based tourism. How tourism can help revive community livelihoods For Preethi, tourism is ultimately about empowering communities by sustaining their livelihoods. “Community-based tourism can create additional economic opportunities while helping communities showcase their culture and knowledge systems,” she says. Visitors could experience both the edible and non-edible worlds of the palmyra ecosystem — tasting fresh palm products and traditional foods while also learning how leaves are transformed into handicrafts, utility products, and decorative items through skills passed down across generations. The benefits, she believes, extend far beyond tourism revenue. Visitors could experience both the edible and non-edible worlds of the palmyra ecosystem — tasting fresh palm products and traditional foods while also learning how leaves are transformed into handicrafts, utility products, and decorative items through skills passed down across generations. Women who already play a central role in producing jaggery, food products, and handicrafts could earn directly from visitors without relying on middlemen. They could price their products themselves, run their own enterprises, and continue living and working within their villages instead of migrating elsewhere in search of employment. “Tourists are not only visitors; they become consumers who understand the work, effort, and knowledge behind these products through direct experience,” says Preethi. That experience also creates a deeper understanding of the communities whose livelihoods depend on the palmyra and of the ecosystem that supports them. Unlike conventional tourism experiences, palmyra communities carry generations of ecological knowledge that exists nowhere else. They know the birds and insects that inhabit the trees, understand seasonal cycles, and recognise changes in flowering and fruiting patterns that come only from living alongside the landscape for decades. “They can narrate these experiences as stories, making the journey more memorable while sharing traditional ecological knowledge associated with the tree,” says Preethi. In her vision, tourism becomes a platform not only for conservation but also for collaboration. Palmyra artisans in Tamil Nadu could exchange ideas with palm-based craft communities elsewhere in the world through co-learning platforms, helping revive traditional practices while encouraging innovation in products and design. She also imagines dedicated celebrations that place the tree at the centre of public attention. “Why not have an exclusive Palmyra Day celebrated globally?” she asks. “The tree deserves recognition for everything it supports.” Greater visibility, she believes, could also encourage more research and development around palmyra products, crafts, and sustainable livelihoods. The outcome, according to Preethi, is not simply economic development but social development as well — one that supports inclusive growth, circular economies, and sustainable tourism models rooted in local ownership. Tourism, she argues, can strengthen the relationship between climbers and the trees they depend on by creating value through cultural experiences, palm-based products, and ecotourism. As communities begin earning more from the living tree, they gain stronger reasons to conserve palmyra landscapes, preserve traditional climbing skills, and protect the biodiversity that exists around them. A tree that cuts across faith What also fascinated her was how the palmyra quietly crosses religious boundaries. Muslim families use palm leaves during wedding decorations. Christian households use them for decorating homes. In Hindu traditions, sweets wrapped in palmyra leaves remain part of festivals like Karthigai Deepam. “It connects people in ways we do not always notice,” she says. The challenge no one talks about For all its benefits, the future of palmyra remains uncertain. The biggest concern is not the tree itself. It is the people. “Most climbers today are around 70 years old,” says Preethi. The younger generation increasingly avoids climbing work due to safety concerns, low earnings, and changing aspirations. As climbers disappear, traditional knowledge risks disappearing with them. “You cannot separate conservation from communities,” she says. “If we want the tree to survive, the people connected to it also need support.” Unlike conventional tourism experiences, palmyra communities carry generations of ecological knowledge that exists nowhere else. Her answer lies in tourism. Not mass tourism, but experiences rooted in local knowledge — trails, festivals, food experiences, and community-led storytelling that create livelihoods while reviving interest in traditional systems. Because for Preethi, saving the palmyra is not only about protecting a tree. It is about protecting everything that climbs with it — livelihoods, culture, memory, and communities that have spent generations looking up at these tall silhouettes and seeing not just trees, but survival.

title: I had to move to Rūātoki to learn te reo Māori. Our tamariki shouldn’t have to
content: Growing up unable to understand her own whānau, Rawinia Higgins went home to Rūātoki and discovered a place where te reo Māori wasn’t simply taught – it was the language of everyday life. Thinking about te reo towns, the theme for Te Wiki o te Reo Māori 2026, my mind goes to Rūātoki – a small town just south of Whakatāne where I learnt to speak Māori. I grew up in an English-speaking home in Wellington. When my native reo Māori-speaking mother and family would get together, they would all be speaking Māori, laughing and sharing stories. I would feel left out because I couldn’t understand and take part in what was being said. When I was around 11 years old, I asked my parents if I could move to Rūātoki – where my mum was from – and attend Rūātoki School. The school was the first officially recognised bilingual school, back in 1978, and was well established by the time I got there in 1985. It was the result of a community where te reo Māori was the norm, staffed by Tūhoe relatives of mine including Koro Whitu McGarvey – who was my teacher – and Tāwhiri and Kaa Williams, among others. It was in this small-town community I learnt te reo Māori – where I was finally able to access the richness of the world that I had been missing. A baptism of fire I won’t romanticise it – learning the language was a baptism by fire. I started out, much to the teasing of my cousins, in the remedial class. I had known of remedial classes at my school in Wellington, but that was for English. At Rūātoki though, the remedial class was for te reo Māori. I still chuckle thinking about it today – it was like living in a parallel universe. What was special about Rūātoki was that it was not only a place where te reo Māori was taught, but also lived in the hearts and homes of the locals every day. That’s the idea behind the te reo towns theme for te wiki this year: to pay homage to those communities who helped create the conditions where te reo Māori could continue to be spoken, learned and lived. They built kōhanga and kura, strengthened whānau and community use of the language, and helped ensure future generations would have access to te reo Māori as a normal part of everyday life. March during Māori Language Week, to demand that the Māori language have equal status with English on August 1, 1980, Wellington. (Photo: Alexander Turnbull Library) It wasn’t consciously political for them and yet it was one of the most politically active decisions they could make. It was about ensuring their children would never have to feel the detachment from culture and community the adults had seen among Māori living in cities. It was about making te reo Māori a normal and natural part of life for younger generations. More than a matter of ‘choice’ It’s important not to simplify this story too much. Rūātoki and other similar communities showed remarkable commitment to te reo Māori, but they were also shaped by circumstance. Around the world, indigenous languages have often remained strongest in communities where people had greater opportunity to live, work and socialise in their own language. Larger towns and cities brought different pressures, with English becoming the dominant language of education, employment, media and public life. This was not a matter of some communities valuing their language more than others or willingly giving it up. Given the choice, most indigenous communities would have wanted to see their language flourish from one generation to the next. The differing fortunes of te reo Māori reflects the uneven impacts of colonisation, urbanisation and social change on people’s ability to use and pass on the language. The lesson is not to romanticise isolation, but to understand the conditions that allow a language to thrive and to recreate those conditions wherever Māori live today. Te reo Māori has come a long way since I went to kura in Rūātoki. It’s now on bilingual signage, in official place names, on our screens, in cafés and restaurants, sports commentary, workplaces and across the public life of this country. Statistics support this, with the 2023 Census recording 213,849 people who could hold an everyday conversation in te reo Māori, up from 185,955 in 2018. That is an increase of 27,894 speakers in five years, and something every New Zealander can take heart in. This growth in visibility is worth celebrating. But visibility is not the same as vitality. A language doesn’t just thrive because it appears on signs, screens or posters. It thrives when people have places to use it, people to use it with, and the words they need for everyday life. Rūātoki, Ōtaki, Matawaia and other te reo towns have always understood this. Te reo Māori grows through whanaungatanga, shared purpose, and communities that make the language normal in the ordinary places where life happens. The gift that Rūātoki gave me Rūātoki didn’t give me just lessons, but a living network of language. The kura mattered deeply, but it was part of something bigger: whānau who spoke, kaumātua who carried the dialect, teachers who believed in the kaupapa, homes where Māori was ordinary, and a community that had decided its children would inherit more than a memory of te reo Māori. There are many te reo towns across the motu, each with their own story, dialect, champions and sacrifices. Rūātoki is just one of them. Ngā Tamatoa and supporters protest at St Kevin’s Arcade, Auckland, 1972 (Photo: John Miller) Te reo towns are not an invention; they are a recognition of communities that have already shown the way. They represent the courage, discipline and love of communities that chose, and had the circumstances, geographical or otherwise, to keep te reo Māori alive in homes, schools, marae and public life. Before there were national strategies and policies, there were communities already doing the quiet, determined work of language revitalisation. They built kōhanga and kura, held hui, corrected and encouraged each other, laughed with each other and kept speaking. They made decisions in kitchens, staffrooms, vans, sports clubs and on marae that would later become a part of a national movement. The challenge now is to keep building the conditions where te reo Māori can live beyond the classroom, ceremony and te wiki. If a language is to thrive, it must have places where it is not only heard but used; not only respected, but shared; not only learned, but lived. I had to go home to find my te reo town. The challenge now is to ensure our tamariki and mokopuna do not have to go searching for theirs. If we keep building the conditions for te reo Māori to thrive, then every town, suburb and community can become a place where the language is not only visible, but ordinary. More Reading

title: The bird that changed Ecuador: how a chance discovery of a rare species helped to save many more
content:
I have to confess that I rarely enjoy birding in montane cloud forests. The birds that live in these mountainous, cool and humid habitats are masters of disguise, usually passing themselves off as a leaf or other form of foliage. But if I want to see antpittas – elusive, ground-dwelling birds that rarely show themselves – then I have no choice.
So, on a cool, cloudy morning my guide, Juan Carlos Crespo, Fredy Ramón Castillo, a local ranger, and I are standing on a steep, muddy path close to Tapichalaca Lodge, 2,500 metres above sea level in the eastern Andes, waiting for the jocotoco antpitta to emerge from the undergrowth.
Fortunately, antpittas have a soft spot for food, especially the large, juicy earthworms Castillo has placed on a low branch nearby. He calls the bird, with increasingly loud and urgent shouts of “venga, venga!” (“come on, come on!”). The minutes tick by, until I begin to wonder if this is a lost cause.
Then, out of nowhere, a plump, thrush-sized bird with a chestnut back, grey front, black crown and white face-patch materialises just a few feet away. It proceeds to gulp down the earthworms as if it has not eaten for days.
I have seen a lot of different birds, but never one that so changed the course of bird conservation. In November 1997, a group led by the influential US ornithologist Robert Ridgely was exploring this area of southern Ecuador to see what they could find.
As they ascended a forest trail at dawn, they heard the sound of a bird in the far distance. As Ridgely recalled many years later, “It had this crazy call, sounding like an owl; but we had no idea what it was, and to be honest I never thought we would find out.”
Ridgely walked ahead of the group, and heard the sound much closer than before. He recorded the call and played it back to the mystery creature, which came crashing through the dense bamboo, right out into the open.
“I knew right away that this was something really special, which no one apart from the local people had ever seen – an entirely new species to science.” It was, in fact, one of the greatest ornithological breakthroughs of the late 20th century: while new species are sometimes discovered, they are rarely so large, noisy and so obviously different from other members of their family.
Talking to local farmers, Ridgely discovered that they were familiar with the bird, which they had named “jocotoco” to represent its loud, barking call. Two years later, the species was officially described, and named the jocotoco antpitta; the scientific name, Grallaria ridgelyi, commemorating its proud discoverer.
Ridgely soon realised that if the bird was to be saved from extinction its forest home needed to be urgently protected. He and a group of like-minded friends created an organisation dedicated to saving the bird and its habitat, raising funds from donors in the US and Europe to buy and restore the land. In 1998 the Jocotoco Foundation was born.
Today, the foundation protects and manages 19 reserves throughout Ecuador, covering about 50,000 hectares (193 sq miles), and manages a further 82,000 hectares of privately and communally owned land. Together, these sites are home to more than 1,350 species of birds – that’s 80% of all those found in Ecuador, and an astonishing one in eight of all bird species on the planet, as well as many other plant and animal species. The foundation also works closely with nearby communities, employing local people as park rangers – many of whom grew up on the land they now protect – and through jobs in wildlife tourism.
The model for the foundation’s reserves is simple and very effective. First, it restores habitat by planting a variety of native trees and other plants, or in some places simply allows the vegetation to regenerate on its own. Park guards, all of whom come from local communities, protect the reserves against illegal incursions such as cattle grazing, logging and poaching, aided by new technology including camera traps and audio recorders.
They also use these to monitor the fortunes of key species, while providing nest boxes to encourage them to breed, making up for the loss of natural tree cavities while the old-growth forests are being restored.
A recent study at Canandé, in the Chocó region of north-west Ecuador, revealed that even after deforestation, nature can recover very rapidly. The study showed that in just three decades – a single human generation – of being managed for biodiversity, formerly cleared lands have recovered 90% of the biomass – the weight of all animals – and 90% of the number of species found in nearby mature forests. While the new mix of species is not fully the same as in a mature forest, 75% of the original species present in an old-growth forest have returned.
Mike Parr, the president of the American Bird Conservancy, has no doubt about the importance of this work. “Beyond safeguarding Ecuador’s rarest birds, migrating species and incredible overall biodiversity, Jocotoco’s strategic integration of ecotourism, public awareness, community engagement and scientific research are world class. They have done an amazing job covering the previously unprotected endangered species of Ecuador.”
During recent visits to Ecuador I have visited 10 of the foundation’s reserves, including those in the Chocó region north-west of Quito and Copalinga in the Amazon foothills, along with the Los Petreles reserve on San Cristóbal Island in the Galápagos, a refuge for a critically endangered seabird, the Galápagos petrel.
On a visit to Buenaventura reserve, a restored cattle ranch in the western foothills of the Andes, we went in search of an even rarer bird: the El Oro parakeet. This charismatic parrot was only discovered as recently as 1980, and has a tiny home range, with fewer than 1,000 individuals.
Another early start took us to an open area of grassland and scattered trees where the birds are known to gather. Moments later, we heard a raucous call, and there they were: several flocks totalling about 20 of these emerald-green birds, the males with a distinctive red forehead.
But even this memorable moment was eclipsed by my visit to the Chakana nature reserve, more than 4,000 metres above sea level in the páramo grasslands of the high Andes – yet just an hour south-east of Quito. On an unexpectedly fine and sunny day, against a stunning backdrop of the snow-capped Cotopaxi volcano, we enjoyed closeup views of the Ecuadorian hillstar, a specialist high-altitude hummingbird, along with nine Andean condors soaring right around us, before they rose high into the clear blue sky.
Numbers of the Andean condor, the world’s largest flying bird by a combination of weight and wingspan, have fallen rapidly in recent years, due mainly to deliberate poisoning. But here, these mighty raptors are now returning to their ancestral home.
Dr Martin Schaefer, chief executive of Jocotoco, believes that even in these dark times there is room for optimism. “The power to restore what we have lost is in our hands.”
Ian J Davidson, Americas regional director for BirdLife International, agrees. “By creating a network of protected habitat ‘arks’, Jocotoco has given these remarkable species a genuine chance not only to endure, but to recover and expand beyond their remaining strongholds.
“Their work stands as a global conservation success story, an inspiring example of what determination, science and long-term stewardship can achieve for nature.”
At a time when President Trump has withdrawn US government funding for conservation projects around the world, the Jocotoco Foundation is a classic model of how scientists and local people can work together to save endangered birds and the precious places where they live.
This article by Stephen Moss was first published by The Guardian on 13 September 2026. Lead Image: Thirty years after a US ornithologist first sighted a jocotoco antpitta, the foundation he set up to restore biodiversity is a model for conservation globally.

title: State memorial 100 years after Dromcollogher cinema fire
content:
A State commemoration for the 48 people who died in the Dromcollogher cinema fire has taken place, marking the centenary of one of the deadliest disasters in Irish history.
The tragedy is known locally as 'The Burning'.
Taoiseach Micheál Martin, accompanied by Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport Patrick O'Donovan, officiated at a formal ceremony in Dromcollogher at midday to honour the victims.
On 5 September 1926, around 150 people gathered in a makeshift cinema in the Co Limerick town to watch two films.
A candle fell and ignited highly flammable nitrate film during the screening, causing the fire to spread rapidly through the temporary venue, which was located upstairs in a large wooden loft.
A wooden ladder was the only means of entering and leaving the building.
Those closest to the exit managed to escape, but many others became trapped and the intensity of the blaze made rescue efforts extremely difficult.
Forty-eight people lost their lives - around one tenth of Dromcollogher's population.
More than half of those who died were under the age of 25, including 15 children. The youngest victims were two seven-year-olds.
The disaster has had an enduring impact on the local community and the wider region.
Delilah Shine, a member of the Dromcollogher26 committee, remembers her grandaunt telling her family how she survived the fire.
"My grandaunt was one of the survivors. When we were young, she used to tell us stories about how she escaped out a window.
"We didn't really believe her until we found the National Archives' statement of how she got out the window of the dressing room, which is where most of the victims died in the end," she said.
Pat Lordan's father Paddy survived the tragedy.
"He came to the cinema that night with his friends Jack Fehan and Edward Stack. They were 15 years of age. Edward Stack was about 22 years of age.
"They were at the back of the cinema and Jack Fehan and my father managed to get out with slight burns," he said.
"Edward Stack stayed behind to help other children escape and my father always said his abiding memory is of him lifting children to the window to help them escape. Unfortunately, he lost his life."
Gerry Keyes, chairman of the Dromcollogher 26 group, said today's State commemoration will be "a fitting and respectful tribute" to the 48 people who died and to the families whose lives were changed by the tragedy.
He said the recognition also acknowledged the historical importance of the disaster and would help ensure that an event of both local and national significance is not forgotten.
A century on, the commemoration will bring the community together to remember the lives lost in one of the darkest nights in Dromcollogher's history.

title: In the Rubber Forests, ‘Shanghai Daughter’ Traces a Father’s Past
url: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019060/In the Rubber Forests, ‘Shanghai Daughter’ Traces a Father’s Past

In the Rubber Forests, ‘Shanghai Daughter’ Traces a Father’s Past
SHANGHAI – At the Sept. 19 Shanghai premiere of her feature debut, “Shanghai Daughter,” Shen Zhongmin carried a rubber seed from the forests of the Xishuangbanna Dai Autonomous Prefecture, nearly 3,000 kilometers away in southwestern China’s Yunnan province, where her late father had worked.
“The seed fell from the canopy and struck me as I retraced his life there,” Shen, 41, tells Sixth Tone.
Her father was among the millions of urban Chinese youths “sent down” to work in rural areas under the Down to the Countryside Movement, a campaign that ran from the mid-1950s through the late 1970s. He spent a decade on a state-run rubber farm near China’s border with Myanmar but rarely spoke to his daughter about those years.
Shen, who works professionally as Agnis Shen, first traveled to Xishuangbanna in 2011, the year after her father died. A former culture editor at the Shanghai-based magazine The Bund and the author of “The Traveler’s Desire,” a collection of short fiction. She returned to the region repeatedly, retracing her father’s life and meeting people from his generation.
Nearly a decade after her first trip, those encounters and widespread coverage of a herd of wild Asian elephants wandering north from Xishuangbanna helped inspire the idea for a film. The herd’s journey drew attention to the rubber plantations that had transformed parts of the region’s rainforest habitat.
Blending fiction with documentary methods, “Shanghai Daughter” follows Ming, a fictional Shanghai woman played by Liang Cuishan, as she seeks out her father’s former acquaintances in Xishuangbanna.
She encounters workers’ dormitories facing demolition and a landscape where mining and modern agriculture are replacing former rubber plantations. She also meets rubber tappers, village doctors, ethnic Dai villagers, and ecological researchers, all of whom appear as themselves and recount their own experiences.
“The film asks how we deal with memory,” Shen says. “When you want to understand something from the past but cannot find reliable firsthand records, how do you search for the answers?”
“Shanghai Daughter” had its world premiere in the Panorama section of the Berlin International Film Festival in February and was later selected for the Hong Kong International Film Festival and the Malaysia International Film Festival.
Seven months later, the film’s Shanghai premiere drew at least a dozen former sent-down youths from the city, all now in their 70s. They traveled about an hour by subway to attend.
At the theater, they shared old photographs from their years in Xishuangbanna, including images taken with Shen’s father, Shen Wanxiong, and posed for a group photo with the director.
Among them was Shen Weilong, 73, a former rubber tapper who had worked alongside Shen Wanxiong and describes him as his best friend. Looking at one of the photographs, he jokes, “This one doesn’t show just how handsome he was. If you want to know what he looked like, just look at his daughter.”
As he speaks about his generation, tears well in his eyes. “Our generation is rarely talked about, and now our time is running out,” he says.
Sixth Tone spoke with Shen Zhongmin the following day as she continued a multi-city promotional tour. The interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.
Sixth Tone: Not a single scene in “Shanghai Daughter” was shot in Shanghai. Why did you choose the title, and what does it mean to you?
Shen: “Shanghai daughters” was originally a local term. Villagers near the farms used it for daughters left behind by sent-down youths. Over time, the label seemed to replace each woman’s real name.
Because of my father’s history, I am also, in a sense, a “Shanghai daughter,” and so I went there too. In Xishuangbanna, the phrase took on a double meaning for me. It suggested a kind of twin existence, like looking in a mirror. We seemed to have completely different yet intersecting destinies, one born in Shanghai and the other 3,000 kilometers away in Xishuangbanna.
To me, “daughter” carries something different from either “woman” or “boy.” One of the first Dai expressions my father taught me was “long yin,” meaning “girl.” The image of a girl carries a particular gentleness that can help heal or ease the deep wounds and heaviness behind this subject. The emotional connection extends beyond father and daughter to one girl and another, and one daughter and another.
I did not want to remain trapped within a particular historical wound or view that period only through criticism. I hoped to create something relevant to the present and oriented toward the future, an expression of repair, renewed empathy, and hope.
Sixth Tone: By telling the story from a daughter’s perspective, the film approaches the sent-down youth movement through one family. How does that perspective differ from other portrayals of the movement?
Shen: This is a deeply personal and highly artistic undertaking. It emphasizes experiencing and observing our surroundings and sensory world anew.
While writing the screenplay, I did extensive research. I gathered oral histories, consulted historical archives, and reconnected with researchers at the Chinese Academy of Sciences who study rainforest restoration. But I wanted to hold back those “concrete” materials for as long as possible and put perception first. Thoughts and opinions can easily create divisions, and once expressed, they have their limits. Perception, however, can be shared and remains more open.
Later, an academically minded journalist asked whether this might be related to ecofeminism. I thought the observation was perceptive. It points toward a perspective that moves beyond anthropocentrism and rejects a structure in which “I am the center, and everyone else is the other.”
Sixth Tone: Rubber trees, dragon fruit, and other elements of the landscape recur throughout the film. How did you use them to connect personal memory with the region’s history?
Shen: During my fieldwork in Xishuangbanna, I often walked around whenever I had time. I gradually came to see the landscape itself as a theater. All the legends and stories I had heard, with their intense dramatic and emotional tension, lay silently buried in a small hill in the village.
Generations have cultivated different crops there, from rice and corn to bananas and, more recently, dragon fruit. A small patch of primary forest protected by the Dai people remains on the hillside. Beneath the present landscape lie my father’s old dormitory and the former rubber plantation.
People disappear faster than memories, but stories spanning more than half a century survive in the land’s subtle traces. When you look at the plants and the land and listen to their voices, it feels as if they are telling you stories, though not in a language humans can hear.
I brought the rubber seed to the screening because, to me, it represents a transformation of cause and effect. More than half a century ago, people had little choice but to clear primary rainforest and plant rubber trees to meet the needs of national development. We now understand that this harmed local biodiversity.
A Chinese Academy of Sciences team is rehabilitating degraded rubber groves. Its goal is not to return them to primary rainforest, which would be scientifically unsound, but to rebalance relationships among species. The researchers are restoring poor-quality groves left by haphazard planting and tapping and introducing species that can bridge rubber plantations and native tropical rainforest. By giving the rubber trees a range of “good neighbors,” they can gradually restore the ecosystem’s layers.
To me, they are taking the “effect” of an earlier decision and planting within it a new, positive “cause,” one that may bear better fruit in the future. The relationship between seed and fruit becomes a metaphor for the transformation of cause and effect. I find that deeply inspiring.
Making the film also took me to Malaysia, where I saw some of the country’s earliest rubber trees. Without that initial transplantation, rubber would not have been planted on such a large scale in Xishuangbanna, and many of these stories would not exist.
Sixth Tone: Why did you blend fiction and documentary methods rather than make a conventional documentary centered on your own search?
Shen: I have always felt that the boundary between reality and fiction is unclear, much like the line between dreams and waking life. Historical narratives also have a dreamlike quality for me, something I have explored in my fiction.
If I had relied on documentary methods alone to examine the sent-down youth movement or my relationship with my father, the film would have felt too narrow.
I drew on my own experience to present subjects I have long cared about in a more contemporary, open form. If I had appeared as myself and made a pure documentary, the film would have become too narrow, confined by the standards of historical fact and leaving viewers less room to project themselves into it and experience it openly.
Sixth Tone: How did you approach your father’s past and his former co-workers while making the film? How did they respond after the premiere?
Shen: My father rarely spoke about the decade he spent in Xishuangbanna. People of his generation generally do not talk about those experiences.
You could sense a deep wound behind the way an older audience member spoke yesterday. At times, his questions seemed to judge other people, but they ultimately revealed his own views and emotions.
I didn’t even know my father had tapped rubber. He had never told me what work he did there. Only when I first walked into the plantation did I understand that these were rubber trees and that his generation had planted and tapped them.
At first, I avoided contacting my father’s former co-workers. I knew they would be eager to help and provide a great deal of firsthand material. But the film began with the particular relationship between my father and me. He had told me very little and died before I could learn more, so I went there to search for and reconstruct that missing part of his life.
I also did not want to disturb them for what was, after all, a small personal project. Revisiting those experiences can be extremely painful, especially for some of them.
Since yesterday’s premiere, I have spent all morning replying to their messages. Today, they are gathering for a reunion lunch to discuss the film.
One of my father’s former co-workers wrote: “Thank you to the screenwriter, creative team, and director for bringing a fitting close to our 50 years as sent-down youths.”
Editor: Apurva.

title: Sao Tomé: Open-air Tchiloli theatre continues to thrive
content:
São Tomé and Príncipe
Sporting a range of outfits accessorised with beards, wigs and hats, actors on Sao Tomé perform a medieval European tragedy on the island off Africa's west coast. Brought to the archipelago nation more than 500 years ago by Portuguese colonialists, the tradition of open-air Tchiloli theatre continues to prove popular with residents and tourists to this day.
One of the troop's members believes its popularity comes from its championing of justice.
Marc Carvalho has been in the troop for 35 years, and says, "people love this culture because it speaks about something very real: justice. Justice does not distinguish between rich and poor. Whether one is poor or rich, man or woman, there must be justice. That’s exactly it."
The play's script is in Old Portuguese; it draws from the legends linked to the Carolingian dynasty, which ruled over the majority of western Europe from the eighth to the 10th centuries AD.
Spectators say the themes continue to resonate, which is what has preserved the tradition for so long.
"It conveys a very important message. Basically, it says that justice is something that, how shall I put it, concerns both the poor and the rich. No matter the religion, no matter the social class. In other words, wealth, that sort of thing. Everything has to be fair. Whoever sows evil reaps evil," says Maribel Borja.
It's intense work, with the troop spending several hours performing at a time. But member Jardel Moniz Fernandez says he finds it energising and hopes to one day include his children in the group.
"I have two children, and soon I’ll start teaching my oldest to play the character of Kata, a young boy who, in the play, has to deliver a letter. I’ll start getting him ready now so that he can also be part of the group," he says.
Open-air Tchiloli theatre is now a UNESCO-listed tradition

title: Ministra Rachel Barros visita Casa da Igualdade Racial de Contagem (MG)
content:
A ministra da Igualdade Racial, Rachel Barros, visitou, na terça-feira (15), a Casa da Igualdade Racial de Contagem, na Região Metropolitana de Belo Horizonte (RMBH). Inaugurado no último dia 10, o equipamento é o sexto do país e o segundo de Minas Gerais a integrar o projeto-piloto do Programa Mais Igualdade, do Ministério da Igualdade Racial (MIR).
Casa funciona como espaço de acolhimento, orientação e apoio especializado
A Casa funciona como espaço de acolhimento, orientação e apoio especializado à população negra, comunidades tradicionais e outros grupos atingidos pela discriminação racial e étnica. Entre os serviços previstos estão atendimentos psicológico, social e jurídico a vítimas de crimes raciais e outras violações de direitos.
Durante a visita, Rachel Barros foi recebida ao som de atabaque e berimbau pelo grupo de capoeira Eskiva Brasil. A atividade contou com a presença de representantes da Prefeitura de Contagem, do Conselho Municipal de Promoção da Igualdade Racial (Compir), de comunidades quilombolas, povos de terreiro, congados e reinados.
A unidade integra o Programa Mais Igualdade e o Sistema Nacional de Promoção da Igualdade Racial (Sinapir). O projeto-piloto contempla seis municípios: Fortaleza (CE), Rio de Janeiro (RJ), Pelotas (RS), Salvador (BA), Itabira (MG) e Contagem (MG).
Cinco eixos
As ações desenvolvidas na Casa da Igualdade Racial estão organizadas em cinco eixos. O primeiro é a justiça racial, voltado ao apoio às vítimas de crimes raciais e de outras violações motivadas por discriminação racial e étnica.
O segundo é a inclusão produtiva, que busca ampliar oportunidades de desenvolvimento pessoal e profissional, com prioridade para mulheres negras e jovens negros. Já o eixo de cultura e educação prevê atividades educativas e culturais, especialmente a partir de referências afro-brasileiras.
O eixo convivência comunitária tem como objetivo fortalecer vínculos sociais, identidade e pertencimento das comunidades atendidas. Por fim, a pactuação federativa busca ampliar a articulação entre União, estados e municípios na implementação de políticas públicas de igualdade racial.
O Ministério da Igualdade Racial define as Casas como equipamentos destinados à redução das desigualdades raciais e ao fortalecimento dos vínculos sociais e culturais da população negra e das comunidades tradicionais.
Em Contagem, a Casa está localizada na rua Manoel de Matos, nº 162, no bairro Central Park. O atendimento é gratuito e ocorre de segunda a sexta-feira, das 8h às 17h.
Diálogo com povos tradicionais em Belo Horizonte
Também na terça-feira (15), o Ministério da Igualdade Racial promoveu um encontro com povos e comunidades tradicionais de Minas Gerais no Centro Nacional de Africanidade e Resistência Afro-brasileira (Cenarab), em Belo Horizonte.
O encontro reuniu representantes de povos de terreiro, comunidades quilombolas, reinados e congados. Durante a atividade, os participantes apresentaram demandas ao ministério e destacaram necessidades relacionadas à proteção dos povos tradicionais.
Além do momento de escuta, foram entregues reconhecimentos a pessoas e trajetórias ligadas à preservação da ancestralidade africana e à luta pela igualdade racial.

title: Wildfire strategy doesn't need a winner—with 3 camps fighting for dominance, the system can't keep up with the risk
content:
One of the problems with how America deals with wildfires is the belief that there is one primary strategy that can end the nation's wildfire crisis. Whether that's detecting and putting out every fire fast, increasing logging and forest thinning, or allowing fires to burn under safe conditions, the default choice today is to pour more money and effort into the star approach of the moment.
But an effective wildfire strategy in the face of worsening fire seasons demands a system of actions—interconnected pieces that reinforce one another.
Right now, those pieces mostly are not connected. Research groups, governments and organizations tend to separate into distinct camps, each promoting its own specific strategy. The result is a system that can't keep up with the rising fire risk.
Our team of researchers, along with fire ecologist Jim Menakis, who recently retired from the U.S. Forest Service, has been looking at wildfires from social, ecological and risk-science perspectives to help forest and fire managers and communities in fire-prone areas turn research into practices that can reduce fire-related risks.
We have seen the pitfalls of current fire management approaches and also examples of what actually works.
Three separate camps
Wildfire strategy tends to break into three distinct camps today, each focusing heavily on one approach over the others.
One camp wants to double down on suppressing every ignition quickly and aggressively, contending that it's the surest way to prevent immediate loss. The direction to put out every fire quickly has been a foundation of the U.S. government response to wildfires since the early 1900s and persists despite attempts over the years to change it.
A second camp says the real problem is fuel: flammable vegetation that has been piling up for decades in forests and rangelands because of too much fire suppression.
This group's solution is to scale up forest and brush thinning through logging and controlled burning. Calls for these actions span political administrations, from the U.S. Forest Service's Wildfire Crisis Strategy during the Biden administration to the Trump administration's 2025 executive order calling for the expansion of American timber production and rescinding protections for roadless areas of national forests. But while excessive fuel is a problem, particularly during dry periods, it isn't the only issue.
A third camp says fire is coming regardless, and people have to live with it by accepting and promoting more fire, but allowing it to burn on our terms, when and where it's safe. This is often called managed wildfire. It sometimes includes creating landscapes and communities that can survive and recover from fire.
Each camp tends to operate in isolation from the others, often with its own budget, workforce, practices and culture. These silos can inhibit communication and coordination, which can make fire management less effective.
Success stories at the intersections
The question for fire management shouldn't be "which of the three is right?" It should be "where do they reinforce each other?"
Successful fire strategies combine many approaches to lower risk. If you look closely, you can see some of the ways these methods intersect.
Fuel treatments, such as prescribed burning of vegetation and forest thinning, used in the right locations, don't stop fires on their own, but they can make suppression safer and more effective by lowering a fire's intensity.
Using prescribed burns and forest thinning strategically can also make it safer for managers to allow lower-intensity fire to expand under favorable weather conditions, thereby dampening future fire risk and letting fire play its ecological role in renewing natural systems. A fire meant to spread still needs a safe edge to stop at, and fuel treatments serve this purpose.
And while suppression and the idea of living with fire appear to oppose each other, the same detection and real-time decision tools that let crews hit a fire hard and fast are exactly the tools needed to allow a fire to burn under safe conditions. Living with fire becomes credible only after fuel treatments have lowered risk to communities.
A place where everyone is working together
Wildfire activity has increased markedly across many parts of the U.S. in recent decades, resulting in destruction in communities, harm to water supplies and tragic fatalities. We believe that changing this trajectory requires a shift in thinking, from promoting a single "best" wildfire strategy to designing stronger connections between strategic options.
Building these connections has to begin long before a fire starts, continue while the fire burns and endure long after the fire has ended. It includes how fire research and fire-risk-reduction projects are designed and funded, how communities are brought into planning to build trust and support, and how communities can lessen their vulnerability to wildfires, such as home hardening, developing escape routes and updating land-use codes.
Reducing fire risk isn't solely the responsibility of a single government agency or private entity; all sectors of society must contribute.
This is already happening where people are willing to do the hard work.
For example, the Northern Colorado Fireshed Collaborative brings together federal and state agencies, local governments, water utilities and residents. It coordinates reducing flammable vegetation across land ownership boundaries, prepares homeowners and communities through education and financial assistance for wildfire prevention measures, and organizes response and recovery efforts as one connected system rather than separate ones.
Everyone has a role
The wildfire problem exceeds what any single entity can effectively tackle on its own.
Fire scientists, government agencies and local communities all play a role, which means you do, too. Check whether your area has a fire collaborative or community wildfire protection plan. Show up to public meetings to stay informed, and start making an impact at home by clearing dry brush around your property and helping neighbors do the same.
The path to better strategies is built by people working together, not by policy on a page.

title: Regina Askia-Williams: My 10 Defining Moments from Nigeria to America
content:
